title: coyomap
goal: coyomap is for a developer whose AI coding agent has written more code than they can hold in their head — code that runs fine until the day they need to understand it. It gives that developer a top-down, drillable map of the codebase: an AI coding agent reads coyomap's method (a set of prose prompts), reads the repo, and produces a structured map — what the project is for, who uses it, the ordered walk through its main use cases, then the machine underneath (components, dependencies, the domain model, the flows and calls that connect them). Every claim in the map is anchored to a real file:line, checked by deterministic gates, and attacked by fresh agents that try to disprove it against the code. The map is committed next to the code and pinned to a commit, so it can be diffed and updated as the code changes, and it is read in an interactive C4 viewer served locally, where each box drills down to the source it describes.

glossary.meaning: the state coyomap exists to cure: an agent has generated so much code that the developer has lost track of it, and — like the cartoon coyote past the cliff edge — nothing is under their feet the day they need to understand it
the deliverable: one structured JSON document describing a whole codebase top-down, committed next to the code as .coyomap/project-map.json
the prose instructions an AI coding agent follows to build and maintain a map — the program half of the product, shipped as markdown rather than code
the small manifest installed into a coding agent's skills folder that makes /coyomap reach the method docs and the CLI in this clone
the why/who/what half of a map — goal, glossary, roles, use cases, Happy Path — authored before any code is read
the machine half of a map — components, dependencies, entry points, the domain model, flows and edges
one actor goal with one trigger and one outcome; the join point between the two layers, since each use case has a flow
the map's spine: one end-to-end ordering of use cases that walks the whole product as a coherent story
the inside view of one use case — its ordered steps between components, dependencies, entities and the actor, each step anchored at its own call site
a named step sequence shared by two or more flows, defined once and referenced, so shared machinery is told at one depth everywhere
one module-, folder- or deployable-sized unit of the code with a single purpose — the leaf box of the map
a group of components (or of smaller subsystems) — the altitude above components, grouped by what the system does rather than by tech tier
a real named type in the code, written as a card with its meaning, fields and relations, and rendered as a class diagram
a bounded context grouping entities — the domain-model analog of a subsystem
one project-wide list of typed relationships between components, dependencies and entities, each with a verb, a reason and a witnessed call site
a bare path:line reference to the exact source location that grounds a claim; every element and most claims carry one
a partial map returned by one build agent as JSON; the tooling merges the fragments into the stored model so no agent ever hand-writes it
a mechanical scan of the code tree that reports where the weight is, where symbols are defined, and how many components the tree implies — sizing input, never rows for the map
the component count the pre-index derives from the code tree, with a generous band; landing far outside it means the altitude was misjudged, and a deliberate exception is recorded
the readability budget for one screen — about five boxes per diagram, so a large system is grouped into levels instead of one crowded picture
the commit the map describes, recorded in the map itself, so a later diff knows exactly which code the map was true for
the final build phase: fresh agents that never saw the build reasoning try to disprove each claim against the code, and every refutation is reconciled
what a code diff does to an existing map — which elements it modifies, adds or deletes, and what those ripple to through the edges and flows
the two maintenance moves: analyze reports a diff's impact without touching the baseline; accept patches the map, re-pins it and commits it
refining altitude inside the one map — nesting a subsystem, promoting a component into one, or flattening a level that pulls no weight; never a second map file
the confidence label every claim carries: read in the code, or guessed from naming and docs
the interactive C4 page a local server builds from the model on demand — never a committed file, so it always matches the map

use_cases.name: Install the coyomap skill
use_cases.trigger: A developer clones coyomap and runs `make install`
use_cases.outcome: the skill manifest, with this clone's path baked into it, sits in every coding agent's skills folder, and a repo-local virtualenv holds the `coyomap` command; typing `/coyomap` in any agent now reaches the method.

use_cases.name: Build a baseline map of a repo
use_cases.trigger: The developer types `/coyomap` in a repo that has no map
use_cases.outcome: the agent reads the method, sizes the code tree, fans out to read the repo, and leaves a validated, commit-pinned map (the JSON model, its markdown view and the pre-index) committed in `.coyomap/`.

use_cases.name: Start the local map server
use_cases.trigger: The developer runs `make start` in the coyomap clone
use_cases.outcome: a small local server is listening on 127.0.0.1, offering a landing page that lists every project they have mapped.

use_cases.name: Explore a map top-down
use_cases.trigger: The developer opens a project in the viewer
use_cases.outcome: they read the goal, the Happy Path and the diagrams, and drill from one screen of boxes into the level beneath it, seeing each element's plain-language annotation as they go.

use_cases.name: Open the source behind a mapped element
use_cases.trigger: The developer clicks the code anchor on a box, arrow or flow step
use_cases.outcome: the exact file and line that grounds the claim appears in the code viewer, read from git at the commit the map is pinned to, with the option to hand it off to their editor or GitHub.

use_cases.name: Analyze a code change against the map
use_cases.trigger: The developer edits code and types `/coyomap analyze`
use_cases.outcome: the agent diffs the working tree against the map's pinned commit and writes an uncommitted report saying which mapped elements the change modifies, adds and deletes, and what those ripple to.

use_cases.name: Accept a change into the baseline
use_cases.trigger: The developer is satisfied with the report and types `/coyomap accept`
use_cases.outcome: the agent patches the model in place, re-pins it to the new commit, re-runs the gates, regenerates the markdown view and pre-index, and commits the map beside the code.

use_cases.name: Change the map on request
use_cases.trigger: The developer asks in plain language for a map change ("split this component", "rename that subsystem")
use_cases.outcome: the agent edits the stored model surgically, refusing anything the code does not back, passes the same gates as any other write, and commits the result.

use_cases.name: Check the method's quality
use_cases.trigger: A maintainer runs the eval on a project that already has a map
use_cases.outcome: a fresh map is built with the current method, scored on grounding and a rubric, and compared against the committed baseline, so a method change is reported as an improvement or a regression instead of a hunch.

use_cases.name: Back up a map with its build transcript
use_cases.trigger: The developer runs the backup script against a mapped repo
use_cases.outcome: the map is bundled together with the exact conversation that produced it, found through the session id the build stamped into the map's provenance file.

use_cases.name: See what a change ripples to in the viewer
use_cases.trigger: The developer opens the impact explorer and picks two commits
use_cases.outcome: the diagrams light up with what the diff touched and what that reaches through the map's edges and flows, and each changed file can be read as a diff in place.

subsystems.name: Method & skill
subsystems.purpose: The prose program a coding agent executes: the method docs that tell it how to build, check and maintain a map, plus the small manifest that makes /coyomap reach them. This is shipped as markdown rather than code, and it is as much the product as the tools are.

subsystems.name: Map authoring
subsystems.purpose: Everything that turns an agent's reading of a repo into the stored map: sizing the code tree first, then defining what a map IS and merging the agents' fragments into one canonical document.

subsystems.name: Map model
subsystems.purpose: The definition of a map: the typed document, the vocabularies its fields may use, the anchor format every claim is written in, and the published JSON schema derived from all of it.

subsystems.name: Fragment assembly
subsystems.purpose: The build path from many agents to one file: each agent self-checks its fragment, the assembler merges them by id, and reconcile/fix apply the assignments and corrections that must survive a re-assemble.

subsystems.name: Map checking
subsystems.purpose: The gates a map must pass before anyone trusts it: is it well-formed and do all its references and anchors resolve, do its cited lines really exist in the code, is it self-contradictory, and is it readable at each altitude.

subsystems.name: Map viewing
subsystems.purpose: How a reader actually consumes a map: the model turned into diagrams and tables, served locally, and explored in the browser down to the source line each box stands for.

subsystems.name: Diagram generation
subsystems.purpose: Builds, from the stored model, every diagram and side-panel payload the viewer shows — the context and subsystem drills, the domain class diagrams, the deployment and channel views, and the Happy Path and use-case sequences.

subsystems.name: Browser viewer
subsystems.purpose: The single-page app the reader works in: the diagram canvas and its drill navigation, the info pane for a selected element, the file browser and code viewer, search, and the change-impact overlay.

subsystems.name: Map serving
subsystems.purpose: The small local HTTP server that fronts every mapped project — serving each map's diagram data built on demand, and reading the mapped repo's files from git at the commit the map is pinned to.

subsystems.name: Map lifecycle
subsystems.purpose: Keeping a map true over time: working out what a code diff does to the map and what that ripples to, and preserving a map together with the exact conversation that built it.

subsystems.name: Method-quality eval
subsystems.purpose: coyomap measuring itself: rebuild a map with the current method, judge it on grounding and a rubric, and compare it against the project's committed baseline to say whether the method got better or worse.

subsystems.name: Command front door
subsystems.purpose: The single `coyomap` command every other part is reached through, and the read-only lookup that answers questions about a stored map without opening it by hand.

components.name: Validate semantic-check helpers
components.purpose: The shared helper library the map validator calls for its semantic (non-schema) checks: it decides whether a nesting parent is the right kind, defined, and cycle-free (all blocking), and it computes the opt-in map-fidelity advisories — peer-level directory compression, absent/unreferenced modules, uncovered code files grouped by directory, and the component-count-vs-code-derived-expectation granularity band. It also owns anchor/source resolution (stripping a `:line`, resolving a path against the repo root) and the domain-coverage thresholds, and it re-measures the repo tree itself rather than trusting the pre-index's JSON.

evidence.why: The blocking hierarchy problem: a child whose parent is not the expected kind (component/subsystem must sit under an S, entity/subdomain under an SD) is appended to `problems`, not `warnings`.
Nesting-cycle detection appends to `problems` too — the cycle check, not a depth cap, is what makes the parent walk terminate; over-deep nesting only becomes an advisory warning.
The peer-compression advisory fires when the map individually references fewer than about a quarter of a directory's sibling source subdirs — the 'many modules folded into one box' lost-signal test.

The file-level coverage gap: a code source file is skipped when it is covered by an exact ref, by a referenced directory prefix, or by a recorded 'Coverage exceptions' dir; everything left is reported grouped by directory.
The granularity advisory stays silent inside the +/-40% band around the code-derived expected component count, and only outside it emits the fold-vs-split hint — a zoom anchor, never a verdict.

components.name: Map auditor
components.purpose: The adversarial pass (`coyomap audit`) that makes the map's two layers refute each other: it reads the narrative Happy Path against the mechanism (flows plus backbone edges) and reports contradictions — a `why:` precondition citing a step that does not exist or comes later in the walk, an entity read before any step writes it, a flow whose opening actor is not among the use case's declared actors, a step with no stated precondition while its siblings have one, and step/edge text written as a static dependency instead of an action. Only hard contradictions block (exit 1); everything else is advisory. It then prints the ranked L2 grounding worklist — self-describing 'actually-does' claims that fresh-context skeptics try to disprove against the code — as text or as `--json`.

evidence.why: The blocking rule in one line: the process exits 1 only when some finding carries CONTRADICTION severity — every ADVISORY / WARNING finding exits 0.
A contradiction in practice: a step's `why:` cites a Happy-Path position that comes AFTER it in the walk, so the narrative order refutes its own stated precondition.

The narrative-vs-mechanism cross-check that stays ADVISORY on purpose: a step reads an entity the Happy Path only writes later; component-granular attribution is lossy in both directions, so it advises rather than blocks.
Worklist tier 1 for edges: an `enforces` / `encrypts` verb is filed as security-critical and appended before the dependency, entity, and generic edge buckets.

The self-describing detail that stops false refutations: a component endpoint carries its canonical anchor plus its member entry points, so an umbrella component is never reduced to one arbitrary file.

components.name: Balance reporter
components.purpose: Reports how readable each rendered diagram is: per-diagram fan-out against the 5±2 target (flagging sparse, soft 10-12, dense, single-child, and homogeneous-family screens), the inter-subsystem component-to-component edge matrix with its busiest cross-subsystem seams, and, for each over-dense non-exempt diagram, a deterministic greedy-modularity split proposal printed as an exact 'Direct map change' block with the next free subsystem id precomputed. It never gates — the command always exits 0, and the same engine supplies the always-on advisory warnings the validator appends; a 'Balance exceptions' block in the map durably silences named diagrams.

evidence.why: Advisory by construction: the command's normal path prints the report and returns 0 — only a missing or unparsable map file is an error.
The per-diagram fan-out table, one row per diagram with its child count and flag, printed under the '(target 5±2)' heading.
The inter-subsystem matrix output: the busiest cross-subsystem seams, ranked by how many component-to-component pairs cross each pair of top-level groups.
The split engine's stop condition — greedy merging halts as soon as no merge improves modularity, which is what makes the proposal deterministic rather than tuned.

The durable escape: a line-leading `cadence:` / `store:` / `messaging:` / `isolated:` record (plus plain diagram ids) inside a 'Balance exceptions' extras block adds that token to the skip set, so a justified advisory stops re-firing.

components.name: CLI dispatcher
components.purpose: The front door of the single `coyomap` command: it reads the first word on the command line and hands the rest to that subcommand's implementation, printing the command list for no arguments, help, or an unknown command. Each implementation is loaded only inside its own branch, so the everyday commands (validate, render, serve, dump) never pull in the code-parsing path and keep working on a plain Python install with no third-party package present; when a command that reads a map is given no map file, the dispatcher fills in the standard `.coyomap/project-map.json` location itself so callers can stay terse.

evidence.why: the pre-index implementation is imported inside its own branch — the only path allowed to touch the third-party parser, so no other command loads it
a map-reading command is dispatched with the argument list already passed through the default-map filler, so an omitted map file resolves to the standard location
appends the standard map path when the scan found no positional argument, which is the whole default-map rule
an unrecognised command prints the error plus the usage to standard error and exits with code 2, so a typo fails loudly instead of doing nothing

components.name: Model dump
components.purpose: A read-only lookup over a stored map: it parses the map file and prints either the whole model back as canonical JSON, or exactly one of four fixed slices — what an id is (kind, display name, canonical source, and its members), an element's full stored record, the backbone links into and out of a node, or a group's member records. The slice set is deliberately closed rather than a query language, it refuses more than one slice flag, and it falls back to the standard map location when no file is named.

evidence.why: with no slice flag the entire parsed model is written back out in the canonical serialization — the whole-map read
more than one slice flag is rejected outright, which is what keeps the surface to exactly one fixed slice per run
the links slice scans the map's backbone links by destination and by source, keeping the authored order and duplicates
the id slice returns the resolved kind, display name, canonical source anchor and members for any element id

components.name: Map model & serializer
components.purpose: Defines the exact shape of a project map — which kinds of elements exist, what fields each one carries, and how their ids must look — and is the only place that turns a map into the committed JSON file and back. It always writes the same bytes for the same map so the file diffs cleanly, and it rejects a malformed map by naming the precise location of the bad value.

evidence.why: the single serialization call — fixed key order, indent 2, trailing newline — so the same map always produces byte-identical JSON
loading raises an error naming the exact JSON path of an unknown field, which is how a malformed map is pinpointed
loading enforces each element array's required id prefix, so a wrongly-prefixed id fails at load
rewrites every reference to a renamed element id across the whole map, so a merge never leaves a dangling pointer

components.name: Map grammar & vocabularies
components.purpose: Holds the shared vocabularies the rest of the toolkit agrees on: what an element id looks like, the kinds and purpose groups a dependency can have, the kinds of entry points and who starts them, the verbs used for data relations and for backbone links. It also fills in a value when the author left one blank, so every reader classifies the same row the same way.

evidence.why: an explicitly authored dependency kind wins; otherwise the keyword fallback below classifies it — the single classification rule
folds a drifted entry-point kind spelling back to its canonical seed, so two consumers cannot split the same kind
the one rule deciding an entry point's effective activation, shared by the viewer, the coverage advisory and the eval
derives a dependency's role purely from the verbs of the links pointing at it, so no stored field can drift from the edges

components.name: Anchor & schema utilities
components.purpose: Small shared helpers for the code references a map is built on: deciding whether a source pointer is well formed, splitting it into file and line, judging whether a cited line could plausibly be the line where something happens, and measuring how far a stored pointer has drifted from where reviewers found the code. It also parses third-party Python without leaking that code's own warnings, and generates a JSON Schema of the map for documentation and editor autocomplete.

evidence.why: the one test for a well-formed source pointer — a file reference or a directory reference
returns why a cited line cannot be the acting statement (a definition header, an import, a comment)
computes whether the stored pointer drifts from the line reviewers reported, beyond a tolerance
suppresses the scanned repo's own syntax warnings so they never surface as coyomap output
the schema is generated from the model classes themselves, so it cannot drift from the real shape

components.name: Fragment assembler
components.purpose: Merges the JSON pieces each build agent returns into one canonical map file. It checks every piece against the schema so a bad one fails alone with its name, refuses to silently overwrite when two agents claim the same id, folds away duplicate dependencies, components and links, adds the missing component-to-data links that flow steps imply, applies the reconcile file, and writes the map plus its markdown view.

evidence.why: the merge itself — every piece's arrays are concatenated into one model, in argument order
the same id claimed by two pieces is reported as a conflict naming both, never silently overwritten
creates the component-to-entity link a flow step implies when no piece supplied one
after collapsing two copies of the same component, re-points every reference to the removed id
writes the canonical map file through the one serializer, so validity is guaranteed by code, not by hand

components.name: Fragment linter
components.purpose: The self-check an authoring agent runs on its own piece of the map before handing it back: shape, source-pointer format, per-row rules for links, flows, data relations and channels, that each cited file really exists in the repo, and that every referenced id is defined here or in a supplied id list. Real errors fail the check; judgment-shaped nudges are printed separately and never fail it.

evidence.why: with a repo root given, every cited file is checked to actually exist, catching a wrong prefix at the source
reports ids referenced but defined neither in this piece nor in the supplied id universe — an invented id dies here
advisory nudges are printed on a separate channel, so a heuristic never fails the check
exits non-zero on any real finding, which is what makes the check a gate the agent must clear

components.name: Reconcile & post-assemble fixes
components.purpose: The bulk-edit toolkit for a map. Before assembly it turns path rules ("everything under this folder belongs to that subsystem") into an explicit, checked assignment file; during assembly it applies those assignments and removes refuted links, healing the flow steps that rode them. After the map is written it rewrites source pointers that reviewers found in the wrong place, drops a refuted link, and resolves duplicate data relations — replacing the throwaway scripts each build used to write by hand.

evidence.why: expands path rules into an explicit assignment file, so a huge map's assignments are generated and checked instead of typed
an assignment replaces the stored list rather than appending, which is what makes re-running the build idempotent
removes the refuted backbone links named by the reconcile file during assembly
writes the reviewers' corrected line into the stored link, matching on the full source-verb-target triple so paired links never swap
the no-reviewers pass: flags stored pointers aimed at a line that cannot be the acting statement

components.name: Code pre-index
components.purpose: Walks the repository before the map is built and writes a sizing file: how much code sits in each directory (lines, file counts, how often it changed), where every class and function is defined, import links between parts the agent already named, how many components the code's size suggests, and what the scan could not read. It is advisory input the build agent reconciles, never rows copied into the map.

evidence.why: writes the sizing file holding the weight tree, symbols, imports, expectation and coverage blocks
records every class/function definition by name with its file and line — the symbol index the viewer searches
the file walk that produces the counted set, after generated, vendored and binary files are excluded
the stop rule: a directory small enough to be one component counts as a single expected unit, which is how the expectation is derived
the expectation is computed from the code tree at build time, so it is a code-derived hint rather than anything read back from a map

components.name: Diagram canvas & drill navigation
components.purpose: The screen the reader spends their time on: it draws the map as a diagram, lets them pan, zoom and switch between the view tabs (Happy Path, Subsystems, Entities, Dependencies, Data, Deployment, and the text-only Glossary / Use Cases / System / Tests tabs), and lets them drill into a box to replace the diagram with that box's own card. It remembers where they have been, so back and forward return each view to the exact zoom, position and selection it was left at, and it shows the legend, the breadcrumb and the environment filter around the drawing.

evidence.why: turns the diagram source picked for the current view/drill state into an SVG drawing
writes that drawing into the page — this single line is what the reader actually sees
attaches pan/zoom to the fresh drawing, with wheel-pan and pinch-zoom wired separately at viewer.js:6681
double-click or Option-click on a container box drills in, which pushes a new view instead of opening a popup
every diagram-changing move is recorded on a back/forward stack, the basis of the arrows and the Cmd-arrow shortcuts

components.name: Element info pane & selection
components.purpose: Turns a click on the canvas into readable detail: the selected box or arrow lights up, everything unrelated fades, and the pane under the diagram fills with that element's purpose, its type tags, its use cases, its entry points and its links. Hovering an element previews its meaning without selecting it; Cmd-clicking more elements stacks their cards; and on a use-case flow a small player walks the steps one arrow at a time.

evidence.why: writes the clicked element's detail card into the pane — the operative line of the whole info pane
one atomic step re-glows every selected element, fades the rest, and re-stacks their cards
a multi-selection appends one card per selected element, so Cmd-clicking a second box adds rather than replaces
hovering any box or arrow pops the meaning tooltip, so the map reads without clicking
the flow step player replaces the selection with exactly one flow step, driving the arrow keys and the prev/next strip

components.name: File browser & code viewer
components.purpose: The right-hand side of the window: the mapped repository's real folder tree, shaded by how much of it the map covers, next to a read-only source view with line numbers, syntax colouring and an overview ruler. Selecting an element on the diagram reveals and highlights its file here; clicking a file selects the matching element on the diagram and shows the source scrolled to its line. Files come from the server as of the map's commit, and one control re-opens the shown file in an external editor or on GitHub.

evidence.why: draws the repository tree from the server's response — the file browser's whole content
fetches the selected file's text (or its inline diff) from the server rather than from disk
writes the highlighted source as a numbered-line table, which is what the code pane shows
clicking a tree row that anchors an element selects that element, closing the file-to-diagram loop
hands the file off to the chosen external editor by URL scheme, with the GitHub blob link as the fallback below it

components.name: Map search sidebar
components.purpose: A single 'jump to anything' box on the far left, opened by the magnifier, the slash key or Cmd-K. Typing filters, as you type, over every element name, entity field, glossary term, operational reference row, file, folder and code symbol, plus the free text of every description. Picking a result reuses the viewer's own navigation: an element is selected in the view that draws it, a file opens in the code viewer, a folder opens in the browser, a term flashes on the Glossary. Typing '@' first scopes the search to the symbols of the file currently open.

evidence.why: every named map element becomes a search row whose action selects it in its home view
lazily pulls code symbols from the server, so a class or function the map never names is still findable
clicking a result runs that row's navigation — the one place a search hit becomes a move in the viewer
Enter jumps to the highlighted result, with the arrow keys moving the highlight just above
opening the sidebar builds the index and runs the query, so the first keystroke already has everything to match against

components.name: Change-impact overlay
components.purpose: Lets the reader project a code change onto the map: pick the map's commit against the working tree, or any two commits, choose how far the ripple should spread, and the diagram badges every affected box as added, modified, deleted or rippled. The pane lists everything hit, grouped by kind and clickable; selecting one element explains why it was hit and which files changed; the file browser badges the changed files and can hide the rest; and opening a changed file shows its inline diff instead of the plain source.

evidence.why: stamps the change badge onto each drawn box — the visible result of arming an impact analysis
writes the 'what does this diff impact' summary into the info pane, every row clickable
changing the ripple depth re-projects which elements count as impacted and redraws in place
with an impact armed, opening a changed file requests its inline diff instead of the plain file
records which files changed, which is what puts the change dots in the file browser and feeds its 'changed only' filter

components.name: Method docs
components.purpose: The prose program a coding agent executes to build and maintain a map: dispatch picks the mode (build / analyze / accept / direct map change), method.md drives the build, and the sibling docs spell out the JSON model, the domain cards, the diagrams, and the change-impact lifecycle. It is product, not documentation — the agent reads it and follows it instead of working from memory.

evidence.why: the docs are executable instructions with modes, not reference: an invocation naming build / analyze / accept routes straight to the doc that implements it.
names the gate sequence every write must pass — validate -> audit -> render — which is what makes the prose enforceable by the CLI.
the division of labour with the tools: build agents return structured rows and `coyomap assemble` writes the model; nobody hand-authors the stored file.
the three-step Build / Analyze / Accept lifecycle table that defines what each mode writes and what gets committed.
the template now only documents the generated view's shape (schema v1, ID-based rows), so it is a spec of the rendering, not an authoring form.

components.name: Agent skill manifest
components.purpose: The one file installed into each agent's skills home so that `/coyomap` (and phrases like 'map this repo' or 'change impact') reaches the method. It carries no method content itself: it pins COYOMAP_HOME to this clone's absolute path and sends the agent to method/dispatch.md.

evidence.why: the trigger phrases the agent host matches on — 'coyomap', 'project map', 'codebase map', 'change impact', 'accept the map'.
the whole payload of the manifest: read `__COYOMAP_HOME__/method/dispatch.md` and follow it.
separates the two directories the agent must not confuse — the coyomap clone (docs + tools) versus the repo being mapped (only `.coyomap/`).
install substitutes `__COYOMAP_HOME__` for this repo's absolute path while copying the manifest into each skills home, so the installed copy points straight back here.

components.name: Change-impact engine
components.purpose: Projects an arbitrary git diff onto an existing map: it re-expresses every changed file in the map's pinned line frame (two `-U0` diffs against the pin), resolves each map anchor hosted in that file to a line / symbol / file rung, then applies one pass of typed ripple rules to report every element the change reaches, ranked by strength.

evidence.why: the line-frame translation: a changed file's fate is computed from diff(pin, base) and diff(pin, target), never from a base->target diff directly.
the fate comparison itself — hunks present identically on both sides cancel; only unmatched hunks mark pinned lines as affected.
the resolution ladder in action: an anchor whose lines the frame touches resolves at 'line', else at the enclosing symbol, else at file rung.
consolidates several anchor hits on one element and assigns its strength on the lattice (direct line/symbol/file above ripple, territory last).
the structural ripple walk — a hit component climbs to its subsystem and onward to every ancestor group, once, never re-firing.

components.name: Map backup & provenance
components.purpose: Records which conversation produced a map (session id + minute-precise build time in a committed provenance.json) and, later, bundles the map files together with the exact transcript(s) of those conversations into a timestamped backup folder. It refuses to move a map out of a repo when no conversation could be found to bundle with it.

evidence.why: the stamp writes the session entry into `<repo>/.coyomap/provenance.json`, the committed record a later backup reads.
the safety guard: a MOVE with zero bundled conversations is refused before anything is created, because it would delete the map and defeat the feature.
copy-then-delete ordering — the map files are copied into the backup first, so a mid-run failure loses nothing.
the transcripts are copied (never moved) alongside the map, which is what pairs a map with the conversation that built it.
the recovery path for un-stamped maps: scan the agent's transcripts for the session that actually wrote project-map.md.

components.name: Eval runner
components.purpose: The `coyomap-eval` command and the deterministic run pipeline behind it: reduce a freshly built map to a comparable quality profile (structure counts, validate/audit findings, coverage, granularity), enforce the build-time freeze hash, compare against the blessed baseline, and archive the whole run (map, views, profile, judge report, delta) so it can later be blessed as the new baseline.

evidence.why: the single command dispatches each subcommand (score / run / hash / claims / judge / protocol / bless / compare) to its implementation, imported lazily.
the freeze guard — the run refuses when the map on disk no longer matches the sha256 written at build time, so a post-build edit can never be scored.
the run's verdict comes from comparing the fresh profile against the baseline profile and judge report; with no baseline the verdict is BASELINE.
archives the run directory — model, generated md view, view bundle, profile.json, judge.json and delta.md — as the historical record a baseline is blessed from.
the profile is computed through the same validate/audit model pipeline the product itself uses, so a map is never scored through a second, drifting grammar.

components.name: Eval scoring
components.purpose: Turns two maps into a verdict. The judge half aggregates externally produced LLM verdicts — a majority-of-N skeptic vote per high-risk claim plus median rubric scores — into a judge report with a protocol fingerprint; the compare half applies baseline-relative hard gates and drift bands and returns PASS, DRIFT or REGRESSED.

evidence.why: the verdict precedence that the whole eval reports on — any failed hard gate is REGRESSED, any breached band is DRIFT, otherwise PASS.
the gates are relative, not absolute: a real baseline map carries validate problems, so the rule is 'no new problems'.
the security-specific hard gate — the number of auth surfaces must never drop between baseline and candidate.
the grounding math: a claim's verdict is the majority of usable skeptic votes, so a single dissenter cannot flip it and a tie is refuted.
anchor drift is measured separately from truth — a confirmed claim whose stored `where` is far from the line the skeptics read counts as drift, not as a refutation.

components.name: Map views builder
components.purpose: Turns the loaded map model into its two generated views: the committed markdown file (canonical section order, sections and columns emitted only when the map has that content, bare anchors re-linked so the text view stays clickable) and the graph payload the viewer consumes (nodes carrying their owned files, entry points, stores and lifecycles, deduped edges with their backing fields resolved, and the store-centric Data view). The `coyomap render` command drives the markdown half, writes it next to the map, and registers the project with the local server.

evidence.why: appends one markdown section in the template's fixed order — called only for a non-empty model list, so a small map omits the section entirely
registers a component as a graph node carrying its owned file list, its grouped entry points and its lifecycle lines
rolls a subsystem's or subdomain's files up from its members, so drilling a group's code viewer spans everything it contains
writes the generated markdown view to the requested .md output
registers the rendered project's folder with the serve recents, so the map shows up as a card without a restart

components.name: Map server
components.purpose: Serves every remembered coyomap project from one local loopback-only HTTP server: the shared viewer shell and static assets, each map's view bundle, file tree and code-symbol list, the change-impact endpoints, and file contents read from git at the map's pinned commit (with a scoped `at=` escape for another commit or a guarded working-tree read). It also serves the landing page for adding, reordering and forgetting project folders, and re-reads a map whose file changed on disk so an edit appears on the next refresh.

evidence.why: binds the threading HTTP server to 127.0.0.1 only
refuses any request whose Host header is not loopback — the DNS-rebinding guard that stops a remote page reading local source
checks the map file's mtime on every project request and drops the cached tree/view/symbols when it changed
reads a file's bytes out of git at the requested commit — the pinned-snapshot read behind the code viewer
serves the one generic viewer shell for every project; the per-map data arrives separately from the project's own API

components.name: File browser, recents & diff rows
components.purpose: Builds the viewer's file-browser tree — repo files nested into folders, each row tagged with how the map covers it and with which element a click should select (the file's own element, its owning component, or the nearest mapped ancestor folder) — keeps the remembered-project list in `~/.coyomap/serve-recents.json` so builds and the running server merge instead of clobbering each other, and parses `git diff` output into the numbered add/delete/context rows the code viewer paints.

evidence.why: sets a row's click target: the element defined or owned at that path, else the nearest ancestor folder an element anchors
rolls a folder up to partial coverage when nothing anchors it but a descendant is mapped — what makes the browser double as a coverage view
records a component as the owner of each file it lists, so clicking any owned file selects that component
puts the opened folder at the front of the recents list after dropping duplicate spellings of the same directory
turns one added diff line into a display row carrying its new-side line number

components.name: Map validator
components.purpose: Runs the model-only semantic rulebook over a loaded map: every element defined once, every cross-reference resolving, and the shape rules for flows, entry points, deps, stores, state machines, messaging channels, domain cards and anchor formats. Blocking breakages come back as problems; the judgement calls (balance, completeness, cadence, persistence coverage, isolated components) come back as non-blocking advisory warnings.

evidence.why: reports every id defined more than once — the duplicate-definition block
the reference check: referenced ids minus defined ids, minus the additivity suppressions, is the dangling-reference list
per-step flow rulebook — a step missing an endpoint is a blocking problem
a backbone edge with neither a `where` call site nor `no_call_site` blocks
anchor-format gate: every source-location field must be a bare `path:line`
example advisory — components appearing in no edge and no channel are collected and warned about, never blocked

components.name: Source & coverage grounding checks
components.purpose: The repo-reading half of validation, opt-in behind `--check-sources` / `--check-coverage`: it opens the cited files to prove each anchor really resolves, that a call-site anchor points at an acting statement rather than a def header, import or comment, and that entity and state-machine names actually appear in the file they cite. For coverage it collects the repo paths the map references and re-parses the entities' source directories to spot named types with no entity card.

evidence.why: existence check: each anchor's path must be a real file (or directory) under one of the source roots
reads the anchored line and asks whether it can be the acting statement (advisory drift check)
state names that do not appear in the cited source file are reported as invented or prose-read
anti-synthesized-entity gate: no token of the entity name found in its SOURCE file is a blocking problem
re-measures the domain model — Python classes in the entities' source dirs with no matching entity card
keeps only the repo-relative paths that exist, the reference set the coverage walk compares the tree against

components.name: Validation run & CLI
components.purpose: Drives one validation pass — calls every check in a fixed order, folds in the hierarchy, balance and tree-coverage checks from the sibling modules, and flags a committed `project-map.md` that differs from the view regenerated out of the model. The `coyomap validate` command line parses the flags, loads the map, prints the inventory, the advisory warnings and the blocking problems, and exits non-zero on any problem; `--emit-unclaimed` instead prints a ready-to-paste adjudication block.

evidence.why: the orchestration: each check's findings are appended to the problems or warnings list in turn
the `--check-sources` branch wires the repo-reading anchor existence check in as BLOCKING
the `--check-coverage` branch re-walks the tree and adds the compression/coverage advisories
compares the committed markdown view with the regenerated one — a stale generated file is surfaced
the gate itself: any blocking problem makes the command exit non-zero

components.name: Advisory adjudication readers
components.purpose: Reads the operator's durable decisions out of the map's own `extras` headings so a justified advisory stays quiet on every later run — accepted flow duplications, unclaimed surfaces, persistence and Happy-Path-coverage records, coarse-fold coverage directories, and the per-kind entry-point completeness contract. Each record is parsed only from a line-leading id or path followed by a separator, so prose that merely mentions an id mid-sentence can never silence a check.

evidence.why: collects the flow pairs adjudicated under an 'Accepted duplications' heading
records an id only when the line STARTS with it and a separator follows — the strictness that keeps prose from exempting elements
collects the repo-relative directories recorded under 'Coverage exceptions'
boundary-aware prefix match, so a recorded dir silences its subtree and not a same-prefixed sibling
reads the per-entry-point-kind completeness contract (complete/sampled/partial), folded to the canonical kind spelling

components.name: Viewer graph builder
components.purpose: Defines the graph shape every viewer diagram reads — nodes (with their files, entry points, deployment hosts, store and lifecycle facts), edges, flows, tests and the store-centric Data view — and injects a default subsystem when a map groups nothing, so a component altitude always exists. It also parses a change-impact report into per-element change labels and new edges for the viewer's diff overlay.

evidence.why: injects the synthetic default subsystem and reparents every component under it when the map declares none
classifies one change-impact report row into an added/modified/deleted element entry
collects a report's from|verb|to row as a new edge the diff overlay draws
splits the report's markdown tables with the shared grammar helpers, so parser and validator cannot disagree on table boundaries

components.name: View bundle assembler
components.purpose: Assembles the single JSON payload the browser app fetches per map: every pre-rendered diagram source, the per-arrow crossing lists, the merged graph with diff annotations, the colour table, the header meta line (repo, commit, build time, schema) and the source-link config (repo root and GitHub URL read from git). Each view is included only when the map actually has that content.

evidence.why: builds the ViewBundle, gating each diagram on has_grouping / has_domain / has_subdomains / has_deployment / has_hp
assembles the header meta line from the repo name plus commit/date or the diff summary
annotates the merged graph with each element's change status so the panel and badges can show it
marks an unchanged element downstream of a changed one as rippled for the diff badges
the debug entry point that dumps the same bundle to a JSON file for two-stage inspection

components.name: Context & subsystem diagram generator
components.purpose: Draws the structural altitudes: the Context view (the system, its actors and the external systems it uses, grouped by purpose and with in-process libraries folded into one drillable box), the Subsystems overview with count-labelled crossings, each subsystem's neighbourhood card, and the two-subsystem edge card. It also produces the explanation payloads behind the Context arrows and the crossing lists behind every subsystem arrow.

evidence.why: emits the Context view's collapsed Libraries box holding every in-process dependency
wraps each purpose bucket of dependencies in its own labelled cluster, shared by Context and the Libraries drill
emits the Subsystems overview's inter-subsystem arrow, labelled by the number of component edges it bundles
emits a subsystem card's bridge arrow from a component to the subdomain its data touches
lists, per subsystem-pair arrow, the concrete component-to-component crossings the panel shows

components.name: Domain diagram generator
components.purpose: Draws the domain-model altitudes as class diagrams: the flat Entities view (each entity a box with its fields, key markers, store, retention and lifecycle), the Subdomains overview, each subdomain's neighbourhood card, the two-subdomain edge card, and the bridge card pairing a subsystem with a subdomain. It also draws the reverse link showing which subsystems read or write each entity.

evidence.why: emits one class box per entity, with its fields and its store/retention/lifecycle lines, for the flat Entities view
emits the Subdomains overview arrow, labelled by how many entity relations cross that pair
emits a subdomain card's crossing arrow to a collapsed neighbour subdomain box
emits the reverse bridge arrow from a subsystem box into an entity, counted by the underlying component-to-entity edges
emits the bridge card's concrete component-to-entity link so a click resolves to the real edge

components.name: Deployment & messaging diagram generator
components.purpose: Draws the runtime picture: the Deployment overview (one box per process, product-area containers on big maps, a shared-infrastructure lane banded by role, and process-to-process arrows derived from async channels and cross-process calls), each process's own card, each container's card, and a per-broker channel diagram for the Data tab. It also injects the process boxes into the graph and lists the calls and channels behind every drawn arrow.

evidence.why: emits the one process-to-process arrow per pair, labelled by the channels and calls that cross it
emits a real arrow from each process to the infrastructure it shares with another process
emits a process card's arrow to each subsystem or component that unit runs
injects a view-only process node per drawn deployment unit so its box binds and shows its operational facts
stores the per-broker publisher-to-channel-to-consumer diagram keyed by broker, for the Data tab

components.name: Behavioural flow generator
components.purpose: Draws the behavioural overlay as sequence diagrams: the Happy Path as an ordered walk of numbered messages from each step's actor to the system, and each use case's flow as messages between the actor and the components, dependencies and entities it touches, with shared sub-flows expanded inline in a named block. It emits the matching numbered narrative and actor lists the side panel shows, kept on the same index as the drawn messages.

evidence.why: emits one numbered Happy Path message per step, from the step's actor to the system lifeline
emits one numbered flow message per step between the two elements it connects
wraps an expanded sub-flow run in a tinted block named by a note, without disturbing the message numbering
builds the side panel's narrative row for a step, carrying its own action text, note and call site
replaces a sub-flow reference step by the referenced sub-flow's own steps, the single expansion all three per-flow views consume

deps.name: git
deps.type: version-control system, driven as a local CLI binary via subprocess
deps.used_for: Reads the mapped repo's files at the map's pinned commit, so the viewer always shows the code the map describes; also resolves refs, lists tracked files, produces diffs for the impact explorer, and supplies churn/history for the pre-index. There is no database in this product — git IS the content store the viewer reads from.
deps.alternative: Every git helper degrades instead of failing: a missing binary or a non-repo folder returns an empty result (the pre-index falls back to an os.walk of the tree; the viewer's GitHub target is simply not offered).

evidence.why: The single read-only git call site the whole server funnels through — `subprocess.run(["git", "-C", repo_root, *args])`, no shell, args passed as a list.
`git show <commit>:<path>` is how the code viewer gets file contents — pinned to the map's commit, so local edits never leak into the view.
The pre-index prefers `git ls-files -z` to enumerate authored files (honors .gitignore) and falls back to an os.walk when the folder is not a git repo.

deps.name: Local filesystem
deps.type: the user's disk — plain JSON/markdown files, no database
deps.used_for: Stores every artifact this product owns: the committed map under each repo's `.coyomap/`, the build fragments, the pre-index, the server's recents list under the user's home, and the map backups. The product has no database and no cloud storage.

evidence.why: The recents store writes `~/.coyomap/serve-recents.json` itself — the only state coyomap keeps outside a mapped repo.
A served project is just a folder holding `.coyomap/project-map.json`, read straight off disk.
Backups are written to `<coyomap-home>/map-backups/<project>-<build-time>/` on the same local disk.

deps.name: Claude Code transcript store
deps.type: another tool's live on-disk session log (`~/.claude/projects/*/<session>.jsonl`)
deps.used_for: Supplies the conversation transcript that produced a map, so a backup bundles the map together with the exact session that built it. Read-only and always copied, never moved, because the store belongs to the running agent.
deps.alternative: When a map carries no stamped session, `--search` scans the transcripts for a Write/Edit of a project-map file to recover the session ids; if no transcript is on disk the backup still bundles the map files alone.

evidence.why: Locates a session's transcript by globbing `*/<session_id>.jsonl` under `~/.claude/projects` — a direct read of another product's store.
Matches the repo to its transcript directory by comparing the `cwd` field Claude Code stamps into each transcript entry.

deps.name: jsDelivr CDN
deps.type: public CDN host (cdn.jsdelivr.net) the viewer page loads scripts from
deps.used_for: Delivers the two browser libraries the viewer page needs at load time (the diagram renderer and the pan/zoom control). Every tag is version-pinned with Subresource Integrity, so a tampered file is rejected by the browser; the server itself never talks to this host.
deps.alternative: None — the viewer has no local copy of these bundles, so with no network the diagram surface does not render.

evidence.why: The svg-pan-zoom script tag points at cdn.jsdelivr.net with an `integrity` hash and `crossorigin=anonymous`.
The mermaid UMD bundle loads from the same host, deliberately the UMD build so SRI covers the whole library.

deps.name: cdnjs
deps.type: public CDN host (cdnjs.cloudflare.com) the viewer page lazy-loads from
deps.used_for: Delivers the syntax highlighter (script plus stylesheet) the first time the user opens the in-app code viewer. Loaded lazily rather than at boot, version-pinned and SRI-checked like the head tags.
deps.alternative: The code viewer still shows the file as plain text if the highlighter never arrives — highlighting is an enhancement, not a requirement.

evidence.why: The highlight.js script URL is built against cdnjs.cloudflare.com with a pinned version constant.
The injected `<script>` carries `integrity` and `crossOrigin` before it is appended — the lazy load is SRI-checked too.

deps.name: Web browser
deps.type: the user's browser — the runtime that hosts the whole viewer UI
deps.used_for: Runs the viewer application: fetches each map's bundle from the local server, renders the diagrams, and persists per-user viewer settings in localStorage. The server can also ask the OS to open it on start.

evidence.why: `webbrowser.open(url)` launches the user's default browser at the landing page when `--open` is passed.
Viewer settings (editor target, source root, GitHub URL, panel sizes) live in the browser's localStorage — no server-side settings store exists.

deps.name: GitHub
deps.type: hosted git service — a blob-URL hand-off target for source links
deps.used_for: Opens a mapped element's source in a browser as a portable fallback when no local editor is configured. The repo URL is derived at build time from the `origin` remote, and the blob link is pinned to the map's commit so the line numbers still match.
deps.alternative: Offered only when `origin` is a github.com remote AND the map records a commit; otherwise the target is not even listed and the user picks a local editor instead. The user can override the URL in Settings.

evidence.why: Build time: `git remote get-url origin` is parsed into `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>` and baked into the view bundle.
Runtime: the blob URL is opened in a new tab with `noopener` — the only outbound navigation the viewer performs.

deps.name: Local code editor
deps.type: desktop application invoked through an OS URL scheme (vscode://, cursor://, idea://, zed://, …)
deps.used_for: Opens a mapped element's file at its exact line in the user's own editor. The hand-off is pure browser: a hidden anchor fires the scheme URI and the OS scheme handler does the opening — no server involvement.
deps.alternative: Ten editors ship as presets plus a custom URI template; if nothing usable is configured the viewer falls back to the GitHub blob link, and failing that reopens Settings.

evidence.why: The target table maps each editor to its URI template with `{abspath}`/`{line}`/`{col}` placeholders.
Only a URI whose scheme is in the editor allowlist is ever returned for an anchor — the enforcement point of the hand-off.

deps.name: CPython
deps.type: language runtime, 3.10 or newer, in a repo-local virtualenv
deps.used_for: Runs the CLI, the pre-index, and the map server. The core gate is deliberately stdlib-only, so the interpreter itself is effectively the entire runtime requirement.

evidence.why: `requires-python = ">=3.10"` is the declared floor.
The venv target fails fast with a readable message when the discovered python3 is older than 3.10.

deps.name: pip
deps.type: Python package installer, run as its own process from the Makefile
deps.used_for: Installs the CLI editable into the repo-local virtualenv, with the optional extras. Deliberately targets the repo's own `.venv` so nothing is installed into the user's system Python.

evidence.why: `$(PY) -m pip install -e '$(REPO)[preindex]'` — the install path, always against the repo-local venv interpreter.
The contributor target adds the `dev` extra (pytest + pyright) through the same installer.

deps.name: setuptools
deps.used_for: Builds the distribution: resolves the src-layout (package root `tools/`, plus the separate eval package), declares the two console scripts, reads the version out of the VERSION file, and wheels the viewer's html/css/js as package data.

evidence.why: `requires = ["setuptools>=64"]` with `build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"`.
The non-obvious package-dir mapping (two source roots) that only this backend resolves.

deps.name: tree-sitter
deps.type: Python parsing library — an OPTIONAL extra, imported lazily
deps.used_for: Extracts symbols and imports from non-Python source files during the pre-index. It is the one deliberate exception to the stdlib-only rule and is firewalled: only the `preindex` command may import it, so validate/render/serve stay dependency-free.
deps.alternative: Python files always go through the stdlib `ast`; when the extra is absent the pre-index still runs and simply reports its non-Python symbol coverage as unavailable rather than failing.

evidence.why: Declared only inside the `preindex` optional extra — the core dependency list is empty on purpose.
The dependency firewall: the import happens inside the `preindex` branch, so no other command can pull it in.
The actual lazy import of `tree_sitter.Parser`, built the documented way for compatibility across 0.21-0.25.

deps.name: tree-sitter-language-pack
deps.type: Python package bundling the tree-sitter grammars — same optional extra
deps.used_for: Supplies the per-language grammars the pre-index needs (javascript, typescript, go, java, and the rest). Probed behind a try/except so a missing or broken pack degrades the pre-index instead of breaking it.
deps.alternative: A grammar that will not load raises a LookupError the caller treats as 'no symbols for this language' — the file is still counted, just not parsed.

evidence.why: Declared alongside tree-sitter in the `preindex` extra.
The availability probe imports the pack inside a try/except and reports a boolean, never raising.

deps.name: pytest
deps.type: Python test runner — the `dev` optional extra
deps.used_for: Runs the tool test suite (the repo's own tests plus the eval's), installed into the repo-local venv by the contributor setup target so the gates run against the editable package.

evidence.why: Declared in the `dev` extra, kept out of the runtime dependency set.
`testpaths = ["tests", "eval/tests"]` — the two suites the runner collects.

deps.name: pyright
deps.type: Python static type checker — the `dev` optional extra
deps.used_for: Type-checks the tools package as a contributor gate. Its config only has to add the two source roots, because the package directory name matches the import name.

evidence.why: Declared in the `dev` extra.
`extraPaths` points at `tools` and `eval/tools`, the two src-layout roots.

deps.name: mermaid
deps.type: browser JS library loaded from a CDN with SRI
deps.used_for: Renders every diagram in the viewer from the pre-built diagram sources in each map's view bundle — the Context, container, subsystem, domain, deployment, and flow views are all mermaid output.
deps.alternative: A parse error or a missing baked diagram degrades to an on-page message rather than a blank stage.

evidence.why: The pinned UMD bundle plus its integrity hash — the UMD build is chosen specifically so SRI covers the whole library.
Initialised with `securityLevel: 'loose'` so HTML labels work; the label text is sanitized on the Python side before it ever reaches here.

deps.name: svg-pan-zoom
deps.type: browser JS library loaded from a CDN with SRI
deps.used_for: Adds pan and zoom to the rendered diagram SVG, so a large map stays navigable at any altitude.

evidence.why: The pinned script tag with its integrity hash, loaded in the page head before the viewer module.

deps.name: highlight.js
deps.type: browser JS library lazy-loaded from a CDN with SRI
deps.used_for: Syntax-highlights source files in the in-app code viewer. Loaded on first use rather than at boot, with a per-extension language map choosing the grammar.
deps.package: highlight.js 11.9.0 (viewer.js HLJS_VER constant, script + stylesheet both SRI-pinned)
deps.alternative: An unknown file extension, or a failed load, leaves the file rendered as unhighlighted plain text.

evidence.why: The single pinned version constant both the script and stylesheet URLs are built from.
The stylesheet is injected with its own integrity hash — the theme is fetched from the CDN too, not bundled.
