a coding agent picks up the `/coyomap` skill (or matches its triggers, e.g. "map this repo") and starts reading the method from the manifest
a coding agent picks up the `/coyomap-eval` skill (or matches "eval this map") and starts the method-quality regression run
a browser requests the server root and gets the landing page listing the recent projects
the landing page asks `GET /api/recents` for the recent project folders, re-reading the recents file so a just-built map appears without a restart
the landing page's folder picker asks `GET /api/browse?path=` for a directory's subfolders and which of them hold a map
the browser requests `GET /static/viewer.js` or `/static/viewer.css` — the shared frontend assets, served from an exact-name whitelist
a reader opens a project's map URL `/coyomap/<project>/` and the server returns the generic viewer shell
the browser app probes `GET /coyomap/<project>/api/health` at boot to confirm the server is reachable before revealing the file and code panes
the browser requests a project's whole view bundle — the graph plus every pre-rendered diagram — at `GET /coyomap/<project>/api/view`
the file browser requests `GET /coyomap/<project>/api/tree` for the repo's file tree at the map's commit, overlaid with map coverage
the search box lazily requests `GET /coyomap/<project>/api/symbols` for the code symbols taken from the pre-index
the code viewer requests one file's text at `GET /coyomap/<project>/api/src?path=&at=` — from git at the map's commit by default, or from the working tree
the impact explorer requests `GET /coyomap/<project>/api/impact?base=&target=&…` to project a code diff onto the map
the impact picker requests `GET /coyomap/<project>/api/impactcommits` for the commits around the map's pin
the impact code view requests `GET /coyomap/<project>/api/impactsrcdiff?path=&base=&target=` for one file's inline diff across any two refs
the landing page posts a folder to `POST /api/open` to add a project to the served list
the landing page posts a folder to `POST /api/forget` to remove a project from the recents list
the landing page posts the dragged card order to `POST /api/reorder` to persist the recents order
every GET first passes the loopback-Host check, so a page on another domain that re-points its name at 127.0.0.1 is refused
every POST must carry the `X-Coyomap: serve` header, which a cross-origin page cannot set — the CSRF gate before any recents change
every request under `/coyomap/<project>/` first re-checks the map file's timestamp and drops the cached diagrams when the map changed on disk
the reader clicks a project card on the landing page, which navigates the browser to that map's URL
the reader clicks a top-bar tab to switch view — Happy Path, Use Cases, Subsystems, Entities, Dependencies, Data, Deployment, System, Glossary, Tests (each hidden when the map has nothing for it)
the reader opens the search overlay (the magnifier button, or the `/` key) to jump to any map element, file, or code symbol
the reader opens the Impact popover to pick two commits and project that diff onto the map
the reader switches the side pane between the file browser and the code viewer
the reader clicks the page title to go back to the server's landing page listing all maps
the serve command finishes loading the projects and the HTTP server starts accepting connections on 127.0.0.1, handing each one to its own worker thread
with `coyomap serve --open`, the server opens the landing page in the developer's browser by itself as it starts listening
the landing page's script runs itself as soon as the page loads, fetching the home folder and the recents list
the browser app fetches the map's view bundle at module load, before any other statement runs — nothing in the app can start without it
the browser app probes the server once at load and, on success, reveals and wires the file browser and code viewer

subdomains.name: Map document
subdomains.purpose: The committed map document as a whole — the typed record every other layer reads, plus the declarative directives and proposals that edit it between builds.

subdomains.name: Behavioral layer
subdomains.purpose: The part of the map that answers 'what does this system do, for whom, in what order' — roles, glossary, use cases, the Happy Path spine, and the use-case flows.

subdomains.name: Structural layer
subdomains.purpose: The machine behind the behavior — components, their groups, external dependencies, entry points, the backbone edge list, the async channel catalog, and the citations grounding them.

subdomains.name: Domain-model layer
subdomains.purpose: The map's own picture of the mapped project's data — entity cards with their fields, relations, storage and lifecycles, and the plumbing types deliberately left unmodelled.

subdomains.name: Operational & quality layer
subdomains.purpose: How the mapped system is deployed, watched, secured and configured, plus the map's honesty record — test-coverage gaps, grounding coverage, and preserved freeform sections.

subdomains.name: Code pre-index
subdomains.purpose: The mechanical reading of the source tree handed to a build — the file walk, the symbols and imports found in each file, and the component-count expectation derived from directory size.

subdomains.name: Viewer graph & file browser
subdomains.purpose: The shape the map takes on its way to the screen — drawable nodes and arrows, flows, the change-impact report, the coverage-tagged file tree, and the list of recently opened projects.

subdomains.name: Change impact
subdomains.purpose: What a code change does to an existing map — the raw diff pieces, the per-file picture of which pinned lines moved, each anchor it hits, and the ripple out to neighbouring elements.

subdomains.name: Method-quality eval
subdomains.purpose: The measurements that say whether a rebuilt map got better or worse — the deterministic profile, the judged semantic scores, and the gated comparison against the blessed baseline.

entities.name: ProjectModel

store.notes: the committed source of truth; the markdown map and the served diagram are generated views of it

entities.meaning: The whole map of one codebase — the single committed document holding everything the map knows, in a fixed key order so it diffs cleanly.

entities.name: Role

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: Someone or something that uses the mapped system — a human user or another service — and what they want out of it.

entities.name: GlossaryRow

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: One term of the project's shared language, explained in a line and pointed at the code that owns it.

entities.name: UseCase

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: One thing a role can get done with the system, stated as what starts it and what comes out.

entities.name: HappyStep

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: One position in the ordered walk through the system's main story — a use case shown where it naturally happens.

entities.name: Flow

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: The inside story of one use case — the ordered exchanges between the pieces of the system that make it happen.

entities.name: FlowStep

store.notes: the same shape also fills subflows[].steps[]

entities.meaning: One interaction inside a flow — who talks to whom, what happens there, and the exact line of code where it happens.

entities.name: SubFlow

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: A named run of steps shared by several use cases — written once and referenced, so every flow that rides it stays at the same level of detail.

entities.name: Group

store.notes: the same shape also fills subdomains[]; `tech` is subsystem-only

entities.meaning: A box that holds other boxes — a subsystem grouping components, or a subdomain grouping entities; both use the same shape and may nest.

entities.name: Component

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: One named piece of the mapped system — roughly a module or folder — with what it is for, where it lives, and which files it owns.

entities.name: Dep

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: Something the mapped project relies on but does not own — a database, a queue, an outside service, a framework or a library.

entities.name: Edge

store.notes: one project-wide backbone list; entity-to-entity relations stay on the domain cards

entities.meaning: One claimed relationship in the mapped system — this piece uses, writes or calls that one — with a witness line of code proving it.

relations.how: both endpoints hold an element identifier as plain text — a component, a dependency or an entity — so no typed column can back the arrow

entities.name: EntryPoint

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: A way in to the mapped system — a route, a command, a webhook or a background loop — with who or what starts it and how often.

entities.name: RunRow

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: One command a developer actually types to run, build or test the mapped project, pointed at where that command is defined.

entities.name: EvidenceItem

store.notes: the same shape also fills deps[].evidence[] and tests[].tests[]

entities.meaning: One citation backing something the map says — a line of code plus the reason it proves the claim.

entities.name: MessagingRow

store.notes: name-keyed: nothing points at a channel, so the row itself is the join

entities.meaning: One channel, queue or topic the mapped system passes messages through — who puts messages on it, who takes them off, and what they carry.

entities.name: Entity

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: One domain card — a real named type in the mapped code, with what it means, what it holds, how it relates to its neighbours and where it is stored.

entities.name: EntityField

store.notes: lives only inside its entity card

entities.meaning: One attribute on a domain card — its name, its type, and the small markers saying whether it is a key, a list, or may be missing.

entities.name: EntityRelation

store.notes: authored on the source card only, so a pair is never stated twice

entities.meaning: One typed link from a domain card to another — what kind of link it is, how many of each side, and how it is wired when no field carries it.

entities.name: Store

store.notes: lives only inside its entity card

entities.meaning: Where one domain type physically lives — which datastore, which compartment inside it, and in what way it is kept there.

entities.name: StateMachine

store.notes: the same shape also fills components[].states

entities.meaning: A lifecycle the mapped code really implements — the named states a thing can be in, how it moves between them, and the line that declares them.

entities.name: StateTransition

store.notes: lives only inside its state machine

entities.meaning: One move from one state to another, and what triggers it.

entities.name: NonEntityType

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: A named type in the mapped code that is deliberately NOT a domain concept — plumbing, recorded on purpose so the coverage check does not call it missing.

entities.name: DeploymentRow

store.notes: name-keyed by unit, like a messaging channel

entities.meaning: One running process of the mapped system — where it runs, how it is reached, how it is configured, and which environments it belongs to.

entities.name: VariantTag

store.notes: lives only inside its deployment row

entities.meaning: One environment a deployment unit runs in, together with the manifest line that proves it belongs there.

entities.name: ObservabilityRow

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: One signal the mapped system emits — a log, metric or trace — with where it is produced, where it is read, and what alerts on it.

entities.name: SecurityRow

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: One way into the mapped system that needs protecting — who may reach it, the code that checks that, and what is risky about it.

entities.name: ConfigRow

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: One setting that changes how the mapped system behaves — what it is for, its default, and whether it differs per environment.

entities.name: TestRow

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: One honest statement about testing — which parts of the map this covers, whether they are tested, which suites do it, and what the gap is.

relations.how: the assessed elements are listed as plain-text identifiers and may be of any kind, so no typed column backs the arrow

entities.name: ExtraSection

store.notes: inside .coyomap/project-map.json

entities.meaning: A section someone wrote by hand that the map does not otherwise know about, kept word for word so nothing is lost — and the place justified exceptions are recorded.

entities.name: Grounding

store.notes: one object on the map document; absent means no grounding pass ran

entities.meaning: How much of the map's risky claims were actually challenged and how many turned out wrong — the map's own confidence, travelling with it.

entities.name: Reconcile

store.notes: parsed from the JSON file passed to `assemble --reconcile`; the tool never writes it

entities.meaning: A re-runnable list of corrections applied to a map every time it is rebuilt, so a hand fix is never quietly lost on the next build.

entities.name: SetDirective

store.notes: inside the reconcile file

entities.meaning: One bulk assignment applied after a build — put these elements in this group, run them in these units, or file this dependency under this purpose.

relations.how: the directive lists element identifiers as plain text, and whichever property it assigns decides which kind of element is legal

entities.name: DropEdgeDirective

store.notes: inside the reconcile file

entities.meaning: One instruction to remove a relationship the map got wrong, and to say what should happen to the flow steps that were riding it.

relations.how: matched against the backbone list by the triple that identifies an edge, rather than by a stored reference

entities.name: Proposal

store.notes: computed and printed by `coyomap balance`; never stored

entities.meaning: One suggested new group for a diagram that shows too many boxes, with a name seed and the members that would move into it.

relations.how: the suggested group lists the elements it would move as identifier and label pairs, not as typed references

entities.name: WalkResult

store.notes: computed per run; every consumer re-walks rather than reading a stored copy

entities.meaning: The set of real source files found in a repo, and whether git or a plain folder walk found them.

entities.name: Symbol

store.notes: written under `symbols` as name lookups plus line extents

entities.meaning: One definition found in the code — a class or function, its file, and the span of lines it covers.

entities.name: ImportRef

store.notes: written under `imports`; dynamic imports are not captured, so the list is a lower bound

entities.meaning: One import found in the code — which file pulls in which module, and on what line.

entities.name: DirExpectation

store.notes: written under `granularity`; checkers re-compute it from the tree instead of reading it

entities.meaning: How many components one folder should reasonably become, worked out from its size — the anchor that says whether a map is drawn too coarse or too fine.

entities.name: GraphDict

store.notes: built on demand from the map document and served; never committed

entities.meaning: The whole map rewritten for the screen — every drawable box, arrow, flow and side table the viewer needs, in one payload.

entities.name: Node

store.notes: derived from the map document each time the viewer asks

entities.meaning: One box on a diagram — whatever kind of map element it came from — carrying its display fields, the files it covers and the group it sits in.

entities.name: Edge (graph)

store.notes: merged from the backbone edge list and the domain cards' relations

entities.meaning: One arrow on a diagram, carrying everything the drawing needs — its kind, its cardinality, and the real field name to write on it.

relations.how: both endpoints hold a node identifier as plain text, resolved by the viewer at draw time

entities.name: HappyStep (graph)

store.notes: carried straight from the map document

entities.meaning: One Happy Path position as the viewer shows it — a title, the use case it opens when clicked, and why it sits where it does.

entities.name: Flow (view)

store.notes: built per request from the map document's flows and sub-flows

entities.meaning: One use-case story as the viewer draws it, with its steps already resolved for display.

entities.name: FlowStep (view)

store.notes: derived from the map document's flow steps at build time

entities.meaning: One step as the viewer draws it — with each end already marked as either a system element or a person, so the arrow reads correctly.

entities.name: TestRowView

store.notes: resolved on the server so the browser needs no id parsing

entities.meaning: One test-coverage row prepared for the screen, with its targets already turned into readable names.

entities.name: TestTarget

store.notes: lives only inside its test row

entities.meaning: One thing a test row assesses, shown by name, and clickable when it is a box actually drawn on a diagram.

entities.name: DiffDict

store.notes: parsed from the markdown report on demand; the report itself is the artifact

entities.meaning: A change-impact report read back in — which map version it compares to which, what changed, and what new relationships appeared.

entities.name: DiffChange

store.notes: lives only inside a parsed report

entities.meaning: What happened to one map element between two versions — added, changed or gone — with a short note.

entities.name: FileTreeNode

store.notes: rebuilt from the repo at the map's commit each time the browser is opened

entities.meaning: One folder or file in the browsable repo tree, tagged with how well the map covers it and which element a click should open.

entities.name: RecentsStore

store.notes: reloaded before every write so a concurrent build registering a project merges instead of clobbering

entities.meaning: The list of projects the user has opened in the map server, most recent first — the cards shown on its landing page.

entities.name: ImpactCore

store.notes: computed per run; the published artifact is the change-impact report

entities.meaning: One change-impact run — which map version it is measured against, which two code versions are compared, and every changed file it looked at.

entities.name: ImpactFile

store.notes: lives only inside an impact run

entities.meaning: One changed file seen through the map's eyes — where it used to live, what happened to it, and which map anchors it touches.

entities.name: Change

store.notes: read from git per run, never stored

entities.meaning: One entry from the raw list of what git says changed — added, modified, deleted or renamed, and under which name.

entities.name: FileFrame

store.notes: lives only inside an impact file record

entities.meaning: Which lines of a file — as the map saw them when it was built — this change actually disturbs, so an old anchor can be judged fairly.

relations.how: two diffs against the map's pinned version are folded together — a hunk present on both sides cancels, and every remaining one marks the lines it disturbs

entities.name: Hunk

store.notes: parsed from git output per run

entities.meaning: One block of a diff — which old lines it replaces and what replaces them.

entities.name: ParsedDiff

store.notes: parsed from git output per run

entities.meaning: One file's diff after parsing — its blocks of change, or a flag saying the file is binary and cannot be read this way.

entities.name: AnchorRef

store.notes: collected from the map document at the start of every impact run

entities.meaning: One place in the code that the map points at, remembered with which element carries it and which of that element's fields it came from.

entities.name: DirectHit

store.notes: lives only inside an impact file record

entities.meaning: One map anchor the change actually reaches, with how precisely it was reached — the exact line, the surrounding definition, or only the file.

relations.how: one hit is produced per anchor in a changed file, copying that anchor's details rather than keeping a reference to it

entities.name: RippleOptions

store.notes: passed in per run; the defaults keep the noisy links switched off

entities.meaning: How far a change is allowed to spread beyond what it directly touches — which weaker kinds of link to follow, and how many hops.

entities.name: _Impact

store.notes: accumulated per run and serialized into the run's result payload

entities.meaning: The verdict on one map element in a change-impact run — whether the change hit it directly or reached it indirectly, how strongly, and by which path.

relations.how: built from every direct hit on the same element and then strengthened by the ripple rules, keyed by identifier rather than by a stored reference

entities.name: RunResult

store.notes: its parts are archived separately as profile.json, judge.json and delta.md

entities.meaning: One eval run of a rebuilt map — its measurements, its judged scores, its comparison to the blessed baseline, and the verdict that follows.

entities.name: MapProfile

store.notes: written into each run directory and into the blessed baseline, under .coyomap-eval/

entities.meaning: Everything measurable about one built map — how big it is, how clean it validates, how well it covers the code — reduced to numbers two runs can be compared on.

relations.how: every count is computed from a loaded map document at scoring time; only the numbers are kept, not the document

entities.name: JudgeReport

store.notes: written beside the profile in each run directory and in the blessed baseline

entities.meaning: The quality signals only a reader can give — how many of the map's risky claims survived a skeptic, and how it scores on each rubric dimension.

relations.how: the pass rate is the majority outcome over the skeptic votes on each risky statement, which are counted and then dropped, never kept in the report

entities.name: DimensionScore

store.notes: inside judge.json

entities.meaning: One rubric dimension's settled score for a map — the middle value of several independent readers, so one outlier cannot swing it.

relations.how: the middle value of the individual readers' marks on this rubric axis; their separate judgements are not kept

entities.name: GroundingVerdict

store.notes: replayed from the raw verdict file the judging orchestration writes; the aggregated report keeps only the counts

entities.meaning: One skeptic's attempt to disprove a claim the map makes — held, refuted, or could not be checked at all — with the line they read.

entities.name: RubricVerdict

store.notes: replayed from the raw verdict file; only the median survives into judge.json

entities.meaning: One judge's score for one rubric dimension, with the reason and the line of code backing it.

entities.name: JudgeProtocol

store.notes: one object inside judge.json; absent on reports written before fingerprinting existed

entities.meaning: The fingerprint of how a map was judged — which model, how many readers, how many claims, which rubric wording — so scores from different regimes are never compared.

entities.name: DeltaReport

store.notes: rendered into the run's delta.md and printable as JSON; the structure itself is not archived

entities.meaning: The verdict on whether a rebuilt map got better or worse than the blessed one — which hard checks failed, which numbers drifted, and what could not be compared.

entities.name: GateResult

store.notes: inside the comparison report

entities.meaning: One must-not-get-worse check and whether the new map passed it.

entities.name: BandResult

store.notes: inside the comparison report

entities.meaning: One measured number checked against how far it is allowed to move from the baseline before a human should look.

entities.name: JudgeBand

store.notes: inside the comparison report

entities.meaning: One judged quality score checked for a fall against the baseline — a rise is always fine, only a drop counts.

entities.name: GranularityResult

store.notes: one object inside the comparison report

entities.meaning: How far each map's component count sits from the count the code itself suggests — the fair check on whether a map is drawn at the right zoom.

entities.name: Thresholds

store.notes: read from the eval workspace config; global settings merged with per-project overrides

entities.meaning: The tuning for how strict a comparison is — which checks block, how far each number may drift, and how much a judged score may fall.

non_entity_types.name: Extent

non_entity_types.name: Extents
non_entity_types.why: a type alias for the per-file table of symbol line spans, not a class of its own

non_entity_types.name: _Maps

non_entity_types.name: _Dir

flows.title: Build a baseline map of a repo

steps.phrase: reads the method's dispatch doc and picks the Build mode
steps.note: no map file on disk means no baseline, even when git history still holds a committed copy

steps.phrase: routes the pre-index command so the code tree is sized and located before any reading starts
lists the repo's tracked files and reads per-file churn from the commit history
emits a symbol row for every class and function definition it parses
writes the pre-index artifact — weight tree, symbols, expected component count, coverage — beside the map
steps.note: advisory input the agent reconciles, never rows copied into the map

steps.phrase: self-checks each harvest and trace fragment before returning it
steps.note: the agents fan out over the sized tree and each returns structured rows, so a bad row dies in its own author's turn instead of at the lead's validate

steps.phrase: runs the model rulebook's anchor, edge and flow checks over the one fragment
confirms every anchor in the fragment resolves to a real file in the analyzed repo
parses each returned fragment as a partial model, so one malformed fragment fails alone and by name
applies the synthesis assignments — subsystem, subdomain, runs_in, dropped edges — after the merge
steps.note: a re-assemble re-applies the same file, so the assignments survive a rebuild

steps.phrase: serializes the merged fragments into the canonical map document
re-derives the auditor's grounding worklist so each fresh-context skeptic's verdict pairs with the claim it answers
steps.note: the skeptics read the code themselves and report the true call site; this pass only judges the difference

steps.phrase: rewrites each drifted anchor in the stored map and re-serializes it
stamps the session it is running in into the map folder's provenance file, so the map can later be paired with the conversation that produced it
commits the model, its markdown view and the pre-index into the repo's map folder, pinned to the build commit

flows.title: Analyze a code change against the map

steps.phrase: reads the change-impact doc, which scopes the work to the diff against the pinned baseline instead of a rebuild
reads the baseline's pinned commit off the stored map — the left end of every diff
steps.note: the baseline is left untouched here; it lags the code on purpose, and that lag is exactly what the report describes

steps.phrase: diffs the pin against the working tree with rename detection, and lists the untracked files on their own
steps.note: the right end is the working tree, so uncommitted edits count; a plain diff omits untracked files, so those are listed separately and treated as added

steps.phrase: places every changed file on at least the component that owns it, sharpening to an entity or a flow step only where reading the code allows
steps.note: the report states the resolution each change reached rather than faking step-level precision

steps.phrase: follows each changed element's backbone links and flow steps outward to what they reach, instead of asking of every baseline element whether it was affected
steps.note: tracing stops honestly at an injection seam, where callers hit a port rather than the implementation

steps.phrase: writes the report under `.coyomap/analysis-changes/<date>.md`, carrying the exact was → now text of every element it touches
steps.note: patch-complete on purpose — accept transcribes this text and reads no code of its own

steps.phrase: hands back a report that is on disk but uncommitted, so it survives a lost session and can be reviewed, shared or accepted later

flows.title: Accept a change into the baseline

steps.phrase: reads the accept half of the change-impact method, which forbids any fresh reading of code at accept time
steps.note: if accept finds itself inferring, the report was incomplete — regenerate the report rather than invent here

steps.phrase: transcribes the report's was → now blocks into the stored map as surgical field edits, never a rebuild
steps.note: the new baseline is the old one patched in place, so its own diff shows real semantic deltas and no wording drift

steps.phrase: reads the new code commit and its date, after checking that the code itself is committed
steps.note: the pin gate: the map and the report are expected to be dirty — that is what this step commits — and a `-dirty` pin is recorded only if the developer picks that option

steps.phrase: re-pins the map to that commit, so the baseline again describes exactly one past commit
re-stamps the map's provenance with this accept session and the repo's current sha
re-runs the map gates over the patched map, because a hand patch can introduce a contradiction the report never had
rebuilds the code pre-index at the new pin, so its line anchors match the re-pinned map
steps.note: only when the map already has a pre-index; skipping it leaves the viewer's symbol search on stale lines for exactly the files the change touched

steps.phrase: commits the map, the markdown view, the pre-index, the provenance and the report together with the code
steps.note: the commit IS the acceptance — it is what keeps the baseline pin aligned with the code commit

steps.phrase: reports the local URL that opens the re-pinned map in the map server
reads the dispatch program's direct-map-change branch, which sends it to edit the stored map surgically instead of rebuilding it
hands over a ready-to-apply split as an exact direct-map-change block — the new group's id and every member to move onto it
steps.note: only when the request came out of the balance report's over-dense-diagram proposal; the block is a starting point, never applied for the agent

deployment.runs_on: The developer's own machine, on CPython 3.10+ inside the repo-local virtualenv, installed editable so the clone stays the source of truth.
deployment.exposed_as: The `coyomap` console script — one command with sub-commands (preindex, validate, audit, render, assemble, lint-fragment, anchor-drift, fix, dump, reconcile, balance). Invoked by the coding agent following the method, or by hand.
deployment.config_source: Command-line arguments only, defaulting the map path to `.coyomap/project-map.json`. No config file and no environment variables on this path; the optional extras decide whether the pre-index sub-command has its parser available.

deployment.runs_on: The same developer machine, as a long-lived foreground process (`coyomap serve`, usually via `make start`), stdlib http.server with a thread per request.
deployment.exposed_as: HTTP on 127.0.0.1 at the chosen port: a landing page, a shared frontend asset route, and a per-project API (view, tree, symbols, src, impact) under /coyomap/<slug>/.
deployment.config_source: The `--port` and `--open` flags plus any folders passed on the command line; the served project set comes from `~/.coyomap/serve-recents.json`, re-read on every recents request so a freshly built map appears without a restart.

deployment.runs_on: The user's web browser, loading the shared frontend from the local server and two libraries from public CDNs.
deployment.exposed_as: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ for the landing page and /coyomap/<slug>/ for a map; opened automatically when the server is started with --open.
deployment.config_source: The per-map view bundle fetched from the server at boot, overlaid with the user's own settings from browser localStorage (editor target, source root, GitHub URL, panel sizes).

deployment.runs_on: The developer machine, same virtualenv and interpreter as the main CLI; a separate self-contained package that depends on the core but is never referenced by it.
deployment.exposed_as: The `coyomap-eval` console script, run when someone wants a method-quality regression check.
deployment.config_source: Command-line arguments plus the eval bundle shipped in the repo (thresholds and rubric); all output goes to a git-ignored `.coyomap-eval/` directory in the evaluated project.

observability.where_emitted: Every CLI sub-command prints a human summary as it works — the pre-index prints its coverage line (git available, tree-sitter available, files walked), the server prints how many projects it is serving and the URL it is listening on, and errors and skip notices go to stderr.
observability.where_viewed: The terminal of whoever ran the command — in practice the coding agent's tool output, since the agent is the usual caller.
observability.alerts: None. This is a local developer tool with no alerting of any kind.

observability.where_emitted: Each sub-command returns a status the shell sees: zero on success, non-zero when a gate fails, and a distinct code for a usage error such as an unknown command or a bad --port value.
observability.where_viewed: The calling shell, the Makefile, and the agent driving the method — this is the machine-readable signal the method's gates actually branch on.

observability.where_emitted: The validator reports blocking problems separately from advisory warnings, covering schema shape, semantic checks such as nesting kind and cycles, anchor existence, and map-fidelity advisories like code-coverage and granularity bands.
observability.where_viewed: Read in the terminal by the agent, which is required to clear the blocking findings before the map is considered built.
observability.alerts: None — the gate is the exit code, not a notification.

observability.where_emitted: The per-fragment self-check each harvest agent runs before returning, reporting schema errors, anchor format and existence problems, unknown id references, and extra-key convention breaches in one pass.
observability.where_viewed: In the sub-agent's own terminal output, deliberately so the agent that has the context fixes its own rows instead of the lead guessing later.

observability.where_emitted: The adversarial pass over an assembled map: deterministic contradiction checks plus a grounding worklist of claims a skeptic should re-verify against the code.
observability.where_viewed: The terminal, during the method's check phase; the worklist then drives further agent work.

observability.where_emitted: The balance command reports per-diagram fan-out against the target band, the inter-subsystem edge matrix, and advisory split proposals for over-dense diagrams.
observability.where_viewed: The terminal. Its proposals are advisory only — a human decides whether to apply them as a direct map change.

observability.where_emitted: The eval builds a fresh map with the current method, profiles and judges it, and compares it against the project's committed map, producing a delta report scored against declared thresholds.
observability.where_viewed: The terminal and the files written under the git-ignored `.coyomap-eval/` directory in the evaluated project.
observability.alerts: None. There is no CI in this repo — no workflow files exist — so nothing runs these gates automatically; every signal above is produced only when a human or an agent runs the command.

tests_note: The suite was NOT run to build this table — every row is inferred by reading the test files and the code they exercise, never from a coverage run or an observed pass. That means a cited suite may touch a code path without asserting the behaviour named here, and an untested verdict is a reading of the test corpus rather than a proven absence; only running the suite with coverage would upgrade any row to verified.

tests.label: State-changing POST endpoints: CSRF header, request-body cap, open/forget/reorder handlers

tests.why: drives the recents store directly (add / remove / dedupe / persist) — the state the POST handlers mutate, but never through an HTTP POST
reorder semantics asserted on the store object, bypassing the /api/reorder route and its guard

tests.gap: Nothing in the corpus issues an HTTP POST. The custom-header CSRF guard, the 403 it returns when the header is absent, the 64KB Content-Length cap and the malformed-body path, and the /api/open folder gate (must contain a .coyomap/ dir), /api/forget and /api/reorder handlers are all unexercised end to end. This is the product's only write surface reachable from a browser: if the header check regressed to a no-op, every test still passes and any web page the developer visits could add or forget projects — and adding a project makes that folder's git-tracked contents servable.

tests.label: Filesystem browser (/api/browse) — the unconfined path walk

tests.why: asserts the directory lister flags a .coyomap/ folder and offers a parent entry, called as a plain function on a temp dir

tests.gap: Only the lister function is tested, never the route. Untested: that an arbitrary absolute path or ~-expansion is accepted with no root and no allowlist, that a non-directory yields 404, that symlinked directories are skipped and unreadable entries dropped, and that file NAMES never leak (only subfolders). The map itself calls this the weakest surface in the product; the deliberate absence of a containment check is exactly the property no test pins down, so a future change that started returning file names or file contents here would break nothing.

tests.label: DNS-rebinding guard actually enforced on every request

tests.why: table-tests the loopback-host predicate itself: absent Host allowed, localhost/127.0.0.1/[::1] allowed, evil.com and a LAN address refused
drives real HTTP GETs against a live server, but only on the happy path — every request carries a loopback Host

tests.gap: The predicate is tested; the WIRING is not. No test sends a request with a foreign Host header and asserts a 403, on either the GET or the POST dispatch. A refactor that dropped the guard call from either entry point would leave the whole suite green while re-opening the rebinding path to every served repo's source.

tests.label: Editor hand-off URI scheme allowlist in the viewer

tests.why: runs `node --check` over the frontend bundle — a syntax gate only, it never executes a line

tests.gap: The repo has no JS test harness, so the scheme allowlist that keeps a user-typed editor template from putting javascript:, data:, file: or http(s): into an anchor href is completely unexercised, as is the second check the Settings dialog runs on save. This guard is client-side and its only defence is that one allowlist; a typo that widened or skipped it would ship silently, and the whole viewer's behaviour is likewise unasserted beyond the file parsing.

tests.label: Diagram label sanitizer — the single chokepoint against map-supplied script injection

tests.why: asserts relation-label TEXT for foreign keys and keyed-by, i.e. what a label says — not that quotes, backticks, brackets, braces, pipes or angle brackets are neutralised
generates deployment and overview diagrams from built maps, so labels pass through the sanitizer incidentally, but no assertion targets the escaping

tests.gap: No test feeds a hostile name (a `<script>` tag, a quote, a pipe) through label generation and asserts the output is neutralised, and no test asserts that every generator routes its labels through the one sanitizer. The diagram renderer runs with HTML labels enabled, so a single generator that builds a label by hand is a script-injection path into the viewer, driven by text an agent wrote into the map. The map names this as the concentrated risk and nothing pins it.

tests.label: Source read at the pinned commit (/api/src) — traversal rejection and the size cap

tests.why: the path guard: empty, absolute, `..` traversal at head and mid-path, backslash and NUL byte all rejected
real temp git repo — listing and showing a blob at a SHA, with a missing path and an unsafe path both returning nothing
blob size distinguishes file from directory from missing, and refuses an unsafe path before any git call
drives /api/src over HTTP for both the worktree frame and a SHA frame

tests.gap: The guards are well covered as functions and the route is reached over HTTP, but no test asserts the 413 refusal for a blob over the 4MB cap, nor that the size check happens BEFORE the blob is buffered — the ordering that keeps a huge file from being read into memory. Also unasserted: the 400 on a bad path and the 404 on a path absent from the commit, as HTTP status codes rather than helper return values.

tests.label: Working-tree file read — repo containment, .git exclusion, gitignore respect

tests.why: a tracked file and an untracked-but-not-ignored file are both served from the working tree
the three refusals in one place: a gitignored file, anything under .git, and a path escaping the repo root

tests.gap: The named refusals are asserted, but not the symlink case the design calls out — no test plants a tracked symlink pointing outside the repo and checks the resolved real path still refuses it. That is the specific escape the containment check exists for, and it is the one route in the product that touches real disk instead of git objects.

tests.label: Git argument injection through commit values and user-supplied refs

tests.why: the commit validator rejects a leading dash, a `--output=` flag smuggle, a ref name and a path-suffixed SHA; accepts short and full SHAs
the ref resolver over the impact base/target parameters, including injection-shaped input

tests.gap: Both validators are asserted, but nothing asserts the second layer — that git is always invoked as an argument list with no shell, and that the `--end-of-options` terminator is present on the rev-parse call. Those are the defences that hold if the character class is ever widened, and a refactor could drop them invisibly.

tests.label: Validator blocking rules — the gate a wrong map must not pass

tests.why: roughly 186 tests across referential integrity, anchor syntax, entry-point kind and cadence contracts, structured stores, flow-step call sites, sub-flows, use-case and Happy-Path completeness, deployment and coverage walls
the anchor-quality check: a definition-header anchor is flagged, an operative line accepted, and the check stays advisory rather than blocking
the granularity advisory recomputed inside validate, asserted as non-fatal

tests.gap: Every row is built from a synthetic map constructed to trip one rule, so the suite proves each rule fires on its own trigger — it cannot show the absence of a false PASS, which is the failure that matters here (a wrong map shipping as validated). Nothing runs the validator against this repo's own committed map as a fixture, and nothing asserts the process exit-code contract that callers and CI actually branch on.

tests.label: Fragment assembly — duplicate-id refusal, merge determinism, dedup and edge collapse

tests.why: the same id in two fragments is reported as a conflict rather than silently overwritten
the CLI fails on duplicate ids AND writes nothing — the property that keeps a half-assembled map off disk
arrays concatenate, singletons are taken, and conflicting singletons are a conflict
component dedup merges same-file entries and repoints test targets; edges collapse only when call sites match
a malformed fragment fails alone, named by its own path, instead of poisoning the run

tests.gap: The refusal is proven for ids within the fragment set, but not for the crash-mid-write case: no test interrupts the write and checks the previous map survived, and no test asserts the write is atomic. Also unasserted: what happens when a fragment file appears or changes during assembly, and whether the 'writes nothing' guarantee holds for the generated markdown view and pre-index as well as the JSON.

tests.label: Reconcile and fix — the in-place edits to a stored map

tests.why: reconcile directives assign fields and survive a reassemble; unknown ids, wrong kinds and bad parents are rejected; zero-match drops warn without failing
malformed directives are refused at load
apply-drift rewrites a drifted security anchor, leaves paired persists/reads edges alone, and skips an ambiguous multi-where edge
drop-edge removes the edge, reports riding flow steps, heals them on repoint, and errors on a missing edge
the rule language: glob depth, override order, wrong-typed ids reported, rules that match nothing reported, and a leading `**` that cannot sweep the whole map

tests.gap: The transformations are well covered but the WRITE is not. These verbs rewrite the repo's only copy of the map in place: no test asserts the write is atomic, that a failure mid-write leaves the original intact, or that a backup exists. Contrast the archive script, where exactly that rollback property IS tested. A partial write here silently destroys a map that took a full agent fan-out to build.

tests.label: Change-impact engine and ripple — diff parsing, anchor resolution, and what a hit reaches

tests.why: diff parsing, cancelling identical edits, the anchor-resolution ladder, enclosing-extent innermost-wins, renames with and without edits, deletions, untracked files and cross-commit cancellation

a component hit ripples to structure, behaviour and data; data does not chain; entity hits reverse into subdomains; step hits stay inside their use case; sub-flow steps reach every referencing use case
the impact API endpoint end to end
unified-diff line numbering, added files, preamble skipping and the no-newline marker
drift detection on confirmed claims, with the corrected anchor recorded

tests.gap: Ripple rules are asserted on hand-built miniature maps of a few elements. Nothing checks the ripple against a real map at real scale, where the risk is not a wrong rule but an overwhelming or misleading result — the map itself frames a wrong ripple as sending a reader to the wrong code. Also unasserted: the callgraph opt-in's decay behaviour beyond one depth case, and any bound on ripple size.

tests.label: Map backup with its build transcript
tests.gap: No test file references the backup tool at all. The whole use case is unexercised: finding the session id in the provenance file, locating the matching transcript, bundling it with the map, and every failure mode (missing provenance, a session id that matches nothing, a partially written bundle). This is the only path that preserves how a map was built; if it silently produces an empty or mismatched bundle, nothing catches it. Note that the archive script, a DIFFERENT tool, is well covered and is easy to mistake for this one.

tests.label: Installing the skill — manifest path baking and the repo-local environment

tests.why: asserts the method doc still carries the leaf rule — a docs-content check, not an install check

tests.gap: Nothing exercises the install target: that the skill manifest lands in the agent's skills folder, that this clone's path is baked into it correctly, that the virtualenv gets the command, or that reinstalling and uninstalling are clean. A broken install makes the whole product unreachable for a new user, and it is the first thing anyone does. Only the CONTENT of the method docs is checked, never the wiring.

tests.label: Exploring a map top-down in the browser — drill navigation, info pane, search

tests.why: `node --check` parses the bundle so a stray syntax error cannot ship — no execution
a grep-style check that no internal model field name is rendered into the UI
a grep-style check that source links are bound by one delegated listener rather than per render

tests.gap: The repo has no JS test harness by design, so the entire browser viewer — drilling from one diagram level into the next, selecting an element and rendering its pane, the search sidebar — has zero behavioural coverage. The three existing checks are a parser gate and two text greps; they would not notice a drill that navigates to the wrong level or a pane that renders the wrong element. This is the primary way a human consumes a map.

tests.label: Seeing a change ripple in the viewer — the impact overlay

tests.why: the commit picker's data: ancestors and descendants of the pin
one file's inline diff across an arbitrary commit range
the impact endpoint the overlay consumes, end to end

tests.gap: The server half is covered; the browser half is not. Nothing asserts that the overlay lights the right nodes for a given impact payload, that picking two commits drives the right request, or that the in-place diff view renders. A correct payload rendered onto the wrong boxes is indistinguishable from a correct result to every test here.

tests.label: Starting the local map server — bind, startup registration, browser launch

tests.why: stands up the request handler on an ephemeral port directly, bypassing the runner entirely

tests.gap: No test calls the serve runner. Untested: that the bind address is 127.0.0.1 rather than all interfaces (the map states this hardcoded bind IS the access control), the default port and what happens when it is taken, the folders passed on the command line being registered at startup, and the optional browser launch. A regression that widened the bind to 0.0.0.0 would expose every served repo to the network and no test would fail.

tests.label: Accepting a change into the baseline

tests.why: the assemble CLI writes a canonical map plus its generated views — one step of the accept sequence, run on its own

tests.gap: The accept flow is orchestrated by the agent skill, so no test covers the sequence: patch the model in place, re-pin to the new commit, re-run the gates, regenerate the markdown view and pre-index, commit. Untested in particular is the ordering guarantee — that the gates run BEFORE the commit — and what state the map is left in when a middle step fails. This path rewrites the committed baseline, so a partial accept ships a map that no longer matches its pin.

tests.label: Building a baseline map end to end, and the per-fragment lint that gates it

tests.why: anchor and extra misuse in one pass, malformed ids refused at load, unknown references against the id universe, unknown-prefix targets, and the warning-vs-problem split
the completeness family never fires per fragment — the boundary between lint and validate
the lint CLI exit codes
the assemble CLI writes the fragments gitignore and the canonical map with its views

tests.gap: Every stage is tested alone; the build as a whole is not. No test walks pre-index to fragments to lint to assemble to validate on a fixture repo and asserts a committed, commit-pinned map comes out. That means stage-boundary defects — a fragment shape lint accepts but assemble mishandles, or a map assemble writes that validate then rejects — are invisible, and they are exactly the failures an agent hits mid-build.

tests.label: Opening the source behind a mapped element — file tree, coverage overlay, code read

tests.why: the path index strips anchors and skips URLs, resolves collisions leaf-first, and maps owned files to their owner
tree nesting and ordering, coverage shading including the partial case, mapped counts summed at each level, and the click target picking the finest ancestor folder
the git-backed tree built from a real commit
symbol flattening from the pre-index, with missing and malformed pre-index both degrading to empty rather than failing

tests.gap: The backend that finds and serves the file is covered; the claim the use case makes is not. Nothing asserts that clicking a given element's anchor lands on the file and LINE that grounds it — the round trip from a map anchor to a scrolled code view lives entirely in the untested frontend. The hand-off to an editor or GitHub is likewise unasserted.

tests.label: Changing the map on request in plain language

tests.why: rule output feeds the reconcile step unchanged, and the coverage report names elements left unassigned
dedup-relation lists both sides then drops the chosen one

tests.gap: The mechanical verbs are covered, but the use case's stated guarantee — that the agent refuses anything the code does not back, and that a requested edit passes the same gates as any other write — has no test. Nothing asserts that a surgical edit is re-validated before it lands, so an edit that satisfies a directive while breaking referential integrity depends on the operator remembering to re-run the gate.

tests.label: Method-quality eval — profiling, judging, comparison gates and the runner

tests.why: the gate matrix: new validate problems and contradictions regress, coverage and auth-surface drops regress, bands and density collapse, granularity gating the candidate only, judge pass-rate and dimension-score drops, and hard-fail precedence
grounding majority vote with dissenters, ties, failed and unverifiable votes; the sampling cap keeping the highest-risk claims; protocol fingerprinting; median and mean score assembly
exact structural counts, completeness and granularity fields, density ratios, and old baselines without newer fields still loading
first run without a baseline, bless round trip, and the map-hash freeze that refuses a map edited after the run started
the model-format path end to end, including the protocol-cache guard and drift on a protocol mismatch

tests.gap: Judges are injected in every test, so the real LLM call, its prompt-to-parse round trip, retries and malformed-response handling are never exercised — the part most likely to break in practice. Nothing asserts the eval's own conclusion is meaningful: a scoring change that makes every map look good would still pass this suite.

tests.label: Map model, grammar vocabularies, anchors and the JSON schema

tests.why: round-trip identity, deterministic serialization across builds, canonical key order, and every element keyed by id
load refuses a wrong format, wrong types with a path, unknown fields, missing required fields and wrong or suffixed id prefixes
id remapping reaches every referenced site including the store's dep reference
anchor forms (file, file:line, file:range, extensionless, directory) and the drift tolerance rules
the committed schema is not stale, every ref resolves, id patterns carry their array prefix, and a markdown link or retired hash anchor is rejected
edge verbs map to roles per family, dep roles union incoming verbs, and entry-point kind aliases fold without ever folding a minted kind
the retired v1 parser stays deleted and no command dispatches to it

tests.gap: Round-trip identity is proven for maps the suite builds, not for the repo's own large committed map — no fixture asserts it survives a load-and-write byte-identically at real scale. Unicode, very long strings and deeply nested extras are unexercised, and nothing asserts the id-remap covers a field added in future without being updated.

tests.label: Code pre-index — weighting, symbol extraction, imports and compression advisories

tests.why: weights count lines and files, exclude vendored code and lockfiles, and degrade without git
symbol extraction reports all matches for an ambiguous name, records kind and line, and records a parse failure instead of swallowing it
import edges reported as named pairs, dynamic imports honestly reported as a lower bound, and no false positive on a substring match
the compression advisories: collapsed plugins, monorepo layout, small unreferenced folds, and the non-product dirs it skips

tests.gap: Symbol extraction is asserted mostly for Python, with non-Python languages covered by a single present-or-self-reported check — so a silently degraded extractor for another language reads as success. Nothing asserts behaviour on a very large tree, where the pre-index's cost and its truncation choices actually matter.

tests.label: Map auditor and balance reporter — the advisory checks

tests.why: read-before-create and actor attribution stay advisory and never block, guarded against known false positives
the L2 worklist and its tiers: structured stores, messaging, state machines, cadence
the small-map advisory, root and per-subsystem rules, homogeneity, the extras escape hatch, the subdomain forest mirror, graph machinery, naming, and its integration into validate

tests.gap: Both are advisory by design, so the tests prove they do not block — but nothing asserts their output is actionable or that they fire on the real map. An auditor that went quiet on every real defect while staying green here would look identical.

tests.label: Views builder, graph builder and the diagram generators

tests.why: roughly 95 tests over the grouping and diagram-generation rules across context, subsystem and domain diagrams
derived dep roles, injection, overview, environments, cards, process topology from the async catalog, co-residency, the all-in-one fold and the readable-cap container grouping
the data view's entity, relation and store rendering
golden equivalence over a real committed map fixture — the one place a full real map drives generation

tests.gap: Coverage is on generated STRUCTURE, not on whether a diagram is readable or correct to a human — a layout that renders every box on top of another would pass. The golden fixture pins one real map, so a change that improves that map's output while degrading every other shape reads as a pass, and the fixture must be refreshed by hand or it silently ossifies.

tests.label: Recents store and served-project discovery

tests.why: add, remove, dedupe and persist; a missing file reads as empty; an external change made while the server runs is merged rather than clobbered; the same directory reached via a symlink dedupes
loading a valid and an invalid project, and slug collisions resolved while invalid folders are skipped
a map edited while the server runs is picked up; an unchanged map keeps the cached bundle; a broken edit keeps serving the old bundle and retries; a missing file keeps the cache
the served view bundle and its cache, tolerating a malformed change report

tests.gap: The store is mutated from request threads behind a lock, but no test exercises concurrent writes — two simultaneous adds, or a reload racing an add. The dedupe and merge tests all run single-threaded, so a lock removed by refactor would not be caught.

tests.label: Command front door and the model dump

tests.why: version flag, no-args usage, unknown command exit code 2, and dispatch propagating not-found and usage errors for validate, audit, balance, fix and render
the core path does not import the heavy parser dependency — an import-cost guard
resolving a component, group, entity and unknown id; edge slices in and out; group members; and the CLI's whole-dump, id-slice, unknown-id and two-slice-flag error paths

tests.gap: Only a subset of the twelve registered commands is dispatch-tested; the rest are reached only through their own module's tests, so a broken registration or a renamed flag on those would surface at runtime rather than in the suite. grounding.note: Full Phase-4 coverage: all 185 L2 claims from the audit worklist were challenged by 8 fresh-context skeptics that never saw the build reasoning, batched by theme (security, external dependencies + persistence, domain ownership x2, backbone edges x2) and told to default to refuted on doubt. The 14 security claims were judged three times independently with different lenses — read-the-check, attack-the-surface, and prove-the-call-chain — and decided by majority; one skeptic verified them against a live throwaway server rather than by reading. 3 claims were refuted and reconciled: the /api/browse route has no containment of its own (re-anchored to the loopback Host guard that is its real barrier, with the gap stated), the pre-index builds rather than owns its per-directory expectation record, and the backup script copies the map folder without owning the map document (edge dropped). The ref-injection guard was confirmed real but anchored at a copy that never sees user input; its anchor was repointed. All 5 state machines were checked against their declaring lines and none was invented.

blocks.purpose: what the map server accepts, and from whom

rules.statement: The map server answers only callers on the machine it runs on.

sites.why: binds the listener to the loopback address

rules.risk: Any process on the same machine that can reach the loopback interface — there is no authentication, no login, and no token of any kind. The bind address is the only access control: 127.0.0.1 is hardcoded, so the server is unreachable from the network. On a shared or multi-user machine, however, ANY local process or local user can read every served map and every file in every served repo at the pinned commit. Accepted as the trust model of a single-user developer tool, but it is a real surface.

rules.statement: A request whose Host header does not name loopback is refused.

sites.why: refuses the request with 403 before routing it

rules.risk: A web page on an attacker-controlled domain that re-points its hostname at 127.0.0.1 to read the victim's source through the browser. Enforced: a request whose Host header does not name loopback is refused with 403. An ABSENT Host (HTTP/1.0, curl) is allowed on purpose — a deliberate, documented hole, on the reasoning that a header-less request is not a browser-driven rebinding vector.

rules.statement: A page on another origin may not add, forget or reorder a project.

sites.why: requires a custom header a cross-origin page cannot set without a preflight

rules.risk: A cross-origin page in the user's browser trying to add or remove projects behind their back. Enforced by requiring a custom request header a cross-origin page cannot set without a CORS preflight the server never answers. There is no token and no origin check, so the guard rests entirely on the browser's preflight behaviour; a non-browser local client can set the header freely.

rules.statement: A file is read at the map's pinned commit, never from a path that escapes the repository.

sites.why: rejects absolute paths, backslashes, NUL bytes and any `..` segment before reading

rules.risk: Anyone who can reach the loopback server — the viewer page, or any local process. Path traversal is blocked before anything is read: absolute paths, backslashes, NUL bytes and any `..` segment are rejected with 400, and the read then goes through git rather than the filesystem, so only objects that exist in the named commit can come back. A blob over the size cap is refused before it is buffered.

rules.statement: The one route that reads real disk still resolves inside the repository.

sites.why: re-resolves the real path inside the work tree, refusing a symlink that escapes

rules.risk: The impact explorer, which must show the uncommitted side of a diff — the one route that touches real disk instead of git objects. Enforced in layers: the resolved real path must stay inside the repo (so a tracked symlink cannot escape), any `.git` component is excluded, and only files git accounts for — tracked, or untracked but not ignored — are served, which keeps a gitignored secrets file from leaking through the viewer. This is the highest-risk read path in the product; the containment depends on all three checks staying together.

rules.statement: A commit value can never be parsed by git as a flag.

sites.why: accepts a bare hex SHA and nothing else

rules.risk: Whoever writes the map JSON, or a caller passing `at=` on the src route — a value that reaches git's argv. Enforced: only a bare hex SHA is accepted, so a value starting with `-` can never be parsed by git as a flag. Commands are run as an argument list with no shell, which removes shell injection separately.

rules.statement: A branch or revision expression can never be parsed by git as a flag.

sites.why: guards the ref on the path that actually reaches git's argv

rules.risk: The impact explorer's base/target parameters, which accept branch names and revision expressions rather than bare SHAs. Enforced, but NOT where the map first claimed: the guard in the server's own ref resolver never sees a request value (its only caller passes the map's own pin). The user-supplied base/target refs are gated in the impact engine, which rejects a leading dash and requires a revision-shaped character class before `git rev-parse --verify --end-of-options` peels it to a SHA. Verified live: `base=--output=/tmp/pwn` returns 400.

rules.statement: The folder picker walks the whole filesystem; nothing on that route narrows it.

sites.why: the origin guard is the only barrier this route has

rules.risk: Anyone who can reach the loopback server; the landing page uses it to walk the disk. NO CONTAINMENT ON THE ROUTE ITSELF — the weakest surface in the product, and the anchor here is the only barrier that actually applies. Any absolute path is expanded, resolved and listed: `/`, `/Users` and `~/.ssh` all return 200 with a real listing (verified live against a throwaway server). Only directory NAMES leak, never file contents, and symlinked directories are skipped. What protects it is not the route but the loopback bind (serve.py:734), this Host guard, and the absence of CORS headers — i.e. it is safe on a single-user machine and not on a shared one.

rules.statement: A folder is served only when it already holds a `.coyomap/` directory.

sites.why: refuses a folder with no map directory

rules.risk: The landing page, or any local caller that can set the CSRF header. The only gate is that the folder must contain a `.coyomap/` directory. That is a low bar: creating such a directory anywhere makes that folder — and, through the src route, its git-tracked contents — servable. Mitigated by the loopback bind and the fact that reads stay inside a single repo at a pinned commit.

rules.statement: A frontend asset is served by exact name, never by a path.

sites.why: matches the request against a fixed whitelist of names

rules.risk: The browser fetching the viewer's script and stylesheet. Enforced by an exact-name whitelist rather than path joining, so no traversal is possible on this route at all — an unknown name is a flat 404.

rules.statement: An editor hand-off link may only use a scheme on the allowlist.

sites.why: refuses a template whose scheme is not allowlisted

rules.risk: The user, who may type a custom URI template into the viewer's Settings dialog. Enforced in the browser: only schemes on the editor allowlist may land in an anchor href, which blocks `javascript:`, `data:`, `file:` and `http(s):` templates from running script or hijacking navigation. The dialog re-checks the same allowlist on save, so a rejected template is never stored. Note the URI is fired by the page, so the guard is client-side only — a tampered localStorage value is still filtered at the href, which is the right place.

rules.statement: A third-party script runs only when its content hash matches.

sites.why: carries Subresource Integrity on every tag

rules.risk: The two CDNs the page loads its diagram and highlighting libraries from. Enforced with Subresource Integrity on every tag, including the lazily injected highlighter and its stylesheet, so a tampered or swapped file is rejected by the browser. Residual risk: the page still depends on reachable third-party hosts, and there is no Content-Security-Policy header, so SRI is the only barrier.

rules.statement: Text authored in the map is escaped before it reaches a diagram label.

sites.why: escapes label text before the renderer sees it

rules.risk: Whoever authors or edits the map JSON — including an agent writing a fragment. The diagram renderer runs with HTML labels enabled, so label text is a script-injection path in principle. Enforced by a single sanitizer every diagram label passes through, which neutralises quotes, backticks, brackets, braces, pipes and angle brackets before the label reaches the browser. The risk concentrates in that one function: a caller that builds a label without it would bypass the guard.

rules.statement: A request body over 64 KB is not parsed at all.

sites.why: refuses an unstated, zero or oversized Content-Length

rules.risk: Any local caller. Enforced: a missing, zero, or over-64KB Content-Length yields no parsed body, so a large or malformed request cannot exhaust memory. Paired with a 4MB cap on served file contents and a row cap on diff responses.

extras.heading: Balance exceptions
extras.body:
- granularity: 36 components against a code-derived expectation of ~11 (band 6–16). The expectation is bound by the LOC ceiling over a 294-LOC median file, which reads a toolkit of single-purpose stdlib modules as far fewer units than it has. Each component here is one module or one clearly separable unit inside an oversized file (the 2.5 kLOC validator is four; the 2.9 kLOC viewer generator is five; the 6.9 kLOC browser app is five), each with its own job, its own command or view, and its own tests. Folding them to reach the band would hide exactly the pipeline this map exists to explain — the altitude is deliberate.
- store: the entities whose store mode is `transient`, `embedded`, `in-code` or `enum` deliberately carry no `dep`. This project has no database: the only physical store is the local filesystem, already linked on the eight entities that really land in a file. Tagging in-memory view, impact and eval structures with a filesystem dep would state a persistence that does not happen.
- UC2: 16 steps against the 3–15 band. This is the product's whole spine — read the method, size the tree, fan out, self-check each fragment, merge, apply the synthesis assignments, run the gates, ground the claims, stamp provenance, commit. The gate run is already extracted as a sub-flow (SF10) and counts as one; the remaining steps each carry a distinct call site, so compressing further would drop a real anchor rather than reduce altitude.
BLK1: the rules here are a 1:1 migration of the security rows; fusing them is the T7 authoring pass, which has not been run on this map
BLK2: same — a 1:1 migration, not an authored sweep
BLK3: same — a 1:1 migration, not an authored sweep

extras.heading: Coverage exceptions
extras.body:
- tests/: the test suite is measured as coverage of the map's targets in the Tests table, not modelled as components of the product.
- eval/tests/: same — the eval's own test suite.
- assets/: two images used by the README.
- .github/: issue and pull-request templates only; there is no CI workflow in this repo.
- method/templates/: a documentation-only template showing the shape of the generated markdown view.

extras.heading: Unclaimed surfaces
extras.body: - C5: `python -m coyomap.json_schema` prints the generated JSON Schema of the map document. It is a maintainer/tooling surface for regenerating `method/project-map.schema.json` and for IDE autocomplete — no product use case runs it, and the schema it prints is documentation, not a gate (`coyomap validate`'s checks are hand-rolled and semantic). Deliberately off the use-case list rather than a dead surface.

extras.heading: Persistence exceptions
extras.body: - C41: the backup writes a BUNDLE, not a modelled record — a byte copy of the map folder, the conversation transcripts beside it, and a small manifest naming the project and build time. The bundle has no named type in the code (map_backup.py is stdlib-only and never parses the map), so there is no entity to link. This was confirmed by the grounding pass, which refuted the earlier claim that the backup owns the map document.

extras.heading: Audit checks and the L2 worklist
extras.body:
`coyomap audit` exits 1 only on a CONTRADICTION-severity finding (`audit_model.py:593`). Everything else prints and exits 0.

**Blocking (CONTRADICTION)**
- `dangling-why-ref` — a step's `why:` cites a Happy-Path position that is not a step, or a use case that does not exist in the map (`audit_model.py:230`, `audit_model.py:242`).
- `backward-why-ref` — a step's `why:` cites a Happy-Path position that comes AFTER it in the walk (`audit_model.py:234`).

**Advisory / warning (never blocks)**
- `read-before-create` / `read-never-created` — a step reads an entity the walk writes later, or never (`audit_model.py:196`, `audit_model.py:202`). Advisory because component-granular attribution is lossy in both directions (`audit_model.py:142`).
- `forward-uc-why-ref` / `offspine-why-ref` — a use-case id in a `why:` may be ordinary prose, so blocking would fail a build on a sentence (`audit_model.py:256`, `audit_model.py:247`).
- `actor-attribution` — the flow's opening role id is not in the use case's declared actors (`audit_model.py:281`).
- `why-less-step` (WARNING) — a step states no precondition while its siblings do (`audit_model.py:296`).
- `dependency-phrasing` — step or edge text reads as "A needs B" instead of an action (`audit_model.py:318`, `audit_model.py:324`).

Findings print sorted by severity, then check, then location (`audit_model.py:336`).

**L2 worklist ranking** (highest risk first, then deduplicated by claim string at `audit_model.py:510`)
1. Auth-surface protection claims (`audit_model.py:411`).
2. `enforces` / `encrypts` edges — security-critical verbs (`audit_model.py:423`).
3. Component→external-dependency edges (`audit_model.py:430`), skipping deps explicitly folded as framework/library (`audit_model.py:431`).
4. Component→entity ownership edges (`audit_model.py:435`).
5. All remaining backbone edges (`audit_model.py:441`).
6. Appended after the edge tiers: entity store claims (`audit_model.py:458`), messaging-channel publisher/consumer claims (`audit_model.py:471`), state-machine claims (`audit_model.py:483`), and entry-point cadence claims (`audit_model.py:500`).

extras.heading: Entry-point coverage
extras.body:
Attribution convention: every row is anchored on the line that REGISTERS or DISPATCHES the entry point, and belongs to the component that owns that line. So each `coyomap <cmd>` row sits on its `if cmd == …` line in the CLI dispatcher (C30), not on the implementing module's `main`; the only exceptions are the second-level `coyomap fix <verb>` rows (the verb table lives in the fix module, C8) and the two module-only commands that no dispatcher exposes.

- cli: complete — read the CLI dispatcher's dispatch chain top to bottom (12 `coyomap` subcommands), the fix module's verb table (3 verbs), the eval dispatcher's chain (8 `coyomap-eval` subcommands), `[project.scripts]` in `pyproject.toml` (2 console commands), the backup script's argparse subparsers (2), and then a repo-wide grep for `__main__` blocks to catch modules with a runnable `main` that the dispatchers do NOT expose — exactly two: the schema printer and the view-bundle debug dump. Not counted as rows: the global `--version` / `--help` flags, and the `Makefile` targets (`make dev` / `install` / `start`), which are build wrappers around these same commands and have no owning component.
- agent-skill: complete — a project-specific kind for the two agent-invoked skill manifests (`/coyomap`, `/coyomap-eval`); a coding agent, not a human shell, is the caller. Found by listing every `SKILL.md` in the repo (there are exactly two). The eval manifest is filed under the eval runner (C45) because no canonical component lists `eval/SKILL.md`.
- http-route: complete — walked the request handler's path dispatch in the map server end to end: the GET router (root → landing page; `/api/*` → recents + folder browser; `/static/<name>` → whitelisted assets; `/coyomap/<slug>/…` → the shell and the per-project API branch, whose 8 endpoints are matched one by one), plus the POST router's 3-name whitelist. 16 routes. Any other verb falls through to the base handler's 501.
- middleware: complete — the three per-request hooks that run before any route body: the loopback-Host guard on GET, the CSRF-header guard on POST, and the map-staleness refresh on every project request.
- ui-route: sampled — the browser app is a 6900-line single file and was not read in full. Enumerated by grepping it for navigation and listener registrations (`location.`, `history.`, `addEventListener`, `data-view`) plus the button set in `viewer.html`. The app has NO hash routes and NO query-parameter deep links: one URL per project, and all navigation is in-page. The 6 rows cover the landing-page card click, the 10-way view tab bar (one row on the loop that binds every tab), search, the impact explorer, the file/code pane switch, and the title link home. Not recorded: the in-diagram drill gestures, breadcrumbs, back/forward history, the settings and help modals, and the keyboard shortcuts — all reached from inside an already-open view.
- startup-hook: complete — Pass-2 sweep for self-activation across the whole repo: grepped Python for `threading`, `Thread(`, `atexit`, `signal.`, `webbrowser`, `while True`, `cron`/`schedul`, and the browser app for `setInterval`, `setTimeout`, `EventSource`, and the observer APIs. Findings, asserted either way: the map server is the only long-running service, and it self-starts exactly three things — the accept loop (continuous), the thread-per-connection worker spawned by the threading HTTP server (folded into the accept-loop row; its trigger is an inbound request, not a schedule), and the optional `--open` browser launch. The browser app self-runs two boot steps (the view-bundle fetch that gates the whole module, and the one-shot server probe) and the landing page one. There are NO timers, NO polling loops, NO file watchers, NO signal handlers and NO `atexit` hooks anywhere in the repo: the only `signal`-shaped code is the audit vocabulary's word list, the server stops on a caught `KeyboardInterrupt` rather than an installed handler, freshness is checked per request rather than on a timer, the two `while True` loops outside the server are tree walks, and every `setTimeout` in the browser app is a UI animation or flash. `threading` is used only for a lock guarding the recents state.
- Kinds with nothing to record: `webhook`, `mcp-tool`, `job`, `poller`, `event-consumer`, `signal-handler` — no instance of any of them exists in this repo.
- Deliberately out of scope: `internal/` is git-ignored, so its scripts are not part of the committed repo the map is pinned to; the archive helper that lives there is therefore not recorded as an entry point.
